summary: Eritrea has no data protection legislation, no draft bill in progress, and no supervisory authority — it is one of the few African states with essentially no movement toward a data protection framework. There are no statutory duties around lawful basis, transparency, individual rights or breach reporting, and no complaint mechanism for individuals.

The only relevant texts are the unimplemented 1997 Constitution, whose Article 18 guarantees privacy of communications and correspondence but has never been brought into operative force, and the Communications Proclamation No. 102/1998, which regulates telecommunications, broadcasting and post under the Ministry of Transport and Communications rather than protecting personal data as such.

In practice, organizations processing data of Eritrean residents face no domestic compliance obligations, but also operate in an environment with pervasive state control of telecommunications and extremely low internet penetration. Any counterpart obligations will come from foreign law (e.g. GDPR extraterritoriality) rather than Eritrean law.

summary: Estonia is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented by the Personal Data Protection Act (isikuandmete kaitse seadus), adopted in December 2018 and in force since 15 January 2019. The Act covers the areas the GDPR leaves to member states — law-enforcement processing, journalistic and research exemptions, deceased persons' data — and sets the digital age of consent at 13. It also defines the mandate of the supervisory authority, the Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate (Andmekaitse Inspektsioon, AKI) in Tallinn.

Estonia's distinctive wrinkle is procedural: it has no general administrative-fine mechanism, so GDPR penalties of up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover are imposed through the national misdemeanour procedure. This long limited practical enforcement, and the Penal Code was amended on 1 November 2023 specifically to make the higher fine ceilings workable. AKI is nonetheless active through precepts, orders and guidance, in a country whose famously digital government (X-Road, e-residency) makes data governance a high-profile national topic.

For organisations, compliance is standard GDPR practice — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards — with the local nuance that formal fining runs through misdemeanour proceedings rather than pure administrative decisions.

summary: Eswatini's Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 5 of 2022) is a comprehensive, GDPR- and POPIA-influenced law that entered into force in 2022. It applies to data controllers and processors processing personal data by automated or non-automated means in Eswatini, whether or not they are domiciled or headquartered in the country. Rather than creating a standalone regulator, the Act designates the existing telecoms regulator, the Eswatini Communications Commission (ESCCOM), as the Eswatini Data Protection Authority (EDPA), with powers to investigate breaches, resolve complaints and sanction controllers.

Distinctive features include a statutory obligation for all entities that process personal data to register with the EDPA as controllers or processors, a 72-hour personal data breach notification duty, and sanctions ranging from warnings and enforcement notices to suspension of processing and fines of up to E5 million or 2% of annual turnover.

Enforcement is still maturing: ESCCOM/EDPA has been operationalising the regime through public notices and draft regulations (including on controller/processor registration and data protection officers), and there is not yet a significant published track record of fines. Companies dealing with Eswatini should treat registration and breach-notification readiness as the immediate compliance priorities.

summary: Ethiopia's first comprehensive privacy law, the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, was approved by Parliament on 4 April 2024 and entered into force in mid-2024. It is broadly GDPR-inspired — lawful bases, data-subject rights, DPOs, 72-hour breach notification — but with distinctly Ethiopian features: a data-localisation requirement obliging controllers to store locally collected personal data on servers or data centres in Ethiopia, and prior regulator approval for cross-border transfers of sensitive data.

Supervision was assigned to the Ethiopian Communications Authority (ECA) rather than a standalone privacy regulator. The ECA maintains the register of controllers and processors, investigates complaints, issues enforcement notices and can impose administrative fines; the Proclamation also carries graduated criminal penalties, rising to five-to-ten years' imprisonment and fines of ETB 200,000–600,000 for unlawful international transfers. Minors are defined as under 16, and their data requires parental or guardian consent.

Enforcement reality lags the text: a year after entry into force, reporting described a slow path to operationalisation, with implementing directives, registration machinery and ECA capacity still being built. Companies serving the Ethiopian market should nonetheless plan for registration, DPO appointment, the localisation rule and the 72-hour breach clock, as the ECA has been holding implementation workshops and is expected to ramp up.

summary: Fiji has no comprehensive data protection statute, but it is the Pacific state with the strongest constitutional foundation for one: section 24 of the 2013 Constitution guarantees the right to personal privacy, including confidentiality of personal information and communications. In November 2025, Prime Minister Rabuka announced Cabinet's endorsement of a National Privacy and Personal Data Protection Policy, which explicitly lays the foundation for developing national privacy and personal data protection legislation. No bill had been published or tabled in Parliament as of August 2026, so Fiji sits at the policy-endorsed, pre-bill stage.

Meaningful sectoral protections fill some gaps. The Cybercrime Act 2021 covers offences against the confidentiality, integrity and availability of computer data and systems. The Reserve Bank of Fiji's Protection of Consumer Data & Privacy Guideline (February 2024) imposes data-handling standards on licensed financial institutions. Confidentiality duties also arise under the Banking Act 1995, the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service Act 1998, health practitioner and legal profession rules. The National Digital ID program approved in 2024 is also driving codification of data rules around identity systems.

For organisations operating in Fiji today there is no registration, breach notification or cross-border regime and no data protection authority — but constitutional privacy litigation is possible, financial institutions face RBF supervision, and a full statute is now a stated government commitment worth tracking.

summary: Finland is governed directly by the GDPR, specified and supplemented by the national Data Protection Act (1050/2018), which entered into force on 1 January 2019 and replaced the earlier Personal Data Act. The Act exercises GDPR opening clauses on matters such as the processing of personal identity codes, journalistic and academic exemptions, and sets the digital age of consent at 13.

Supervision follows an ombudsman model: the Data Protection Ombudsman and their Office (tietosuoja.fi) act as the national supervisory authority. A distinctive Finnish feature is that administrative fines are not imposed by the Ombudsman alone but by a collegial sanctions board within the office, and public-sector bodies are exempt from administrative fines altogether — a notable divergence from many EU peers.

In practice, compliance in Finland is GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards, with additional care needed around Finnish personal identity codes and employee data (governed by the separate Act on the Protection of Privacy in Working Life).

summary: France applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by the Loi Informatique et Libertés (Law 78-17 of 6 January 1978) — one of the world's oldest data protection laws, comprehensively rewritten in 2018-2019 to fit the GDPR. The national law fills the spaces the GDPR leaves to member states: it sets the digital consent age at 15 (with joint parent-child consent below that), keeps special regimes for health, biometric and criminal-record data, and preserves some prior formalities for sensitive health research processing.

Supervision belongs to the CNIL, the 1978-founded regulator that remains one of Europe's most influential authorities. The CNIL is a prolific enforcer, and notably uses the ePrivacy framework to fine cookie and tracker violations directly — bypassing the GDPR one-stop-shop — which has produced some of Europe's largest penalties against global tech platforms. It pairs enforcement with extensive practical guidance widely used across the French-speaking world.

For most organisations the compliance picture is standard GDPR: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPOs where required, and Chapter V transfer tools. The distinctive French angles are the age-15 rule for minors, strict CNIL cookie-consent doctrine, and active sectoral rules on health data hosting (HDS certification).

summary: Gabon's data protection framework rests on Law No. 001/2011 of 25 September 2011, one of Central Africa's earliest comprehensive statutes, originally modeled on France's pre-GDPR Informatique et Libertés regime: declaration and authorization formalities with a national commission, processing principles, data subject rights, and restrictions on transfers to countries lacking adequate protection. Its longtime regulator was the Commission Nationale pour la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (CNPDCP).

In July 2023 the framework was significantly modernized by Law No. 025/2023, which amends the 2011 law to align more closely with GDPR-era standards. Key changes include transforming the CNPDCP into a strengthened Autorité pour la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel et de la Vie Privée (APDPVP) with enhanced powers, introducing specific protections for children's data, and setting financial sanctions ranging from FCFA 1 million to 100 million.

Enforcement reality is mixed: the authority has an established institutional history (it participates in the NADPA and AFAPDP regional networks) and the 2023 reform signals renewed political attention to the digital sector, but published enforcement actions are scarce and post-amendment implementing practice (breach notification mechanics, DPO expectations) is not yet well documented. Businesses in telecoms, banking and oil services should complete declaration formalities and watch for APDPVP guidance under the amended law.

summary: The Gambia enacted its first comprehensive privacy statute in 2025: the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act was passed unanimously by the National Assembly on 29 September 2025 and assented to by President Adama Barrow on 7 November 2025 — so the country has moved from 'bill in progress' to having a law in force. The Act was developed with Council of Europe support and aligns with GDPR-style international practice: lawful bases, data-subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPOs, and turnover-based fines up to 4% of annual global turnover.

Rather than creating a brand-new agency, the Act vests supervision in the existing Information Commission, established under the Access to Information Act 2021, giving it a dual access-to-information and data protection mandate with powers to investigate complaints, issue guidelines and impose administrative fines. Criminal sanctions range from GMD 500,000 for unlawful processing up to GMD 10 million and 10 years' imprisonment for aggravated offences such as unlawful data sales.

Distinctive points: children are defined as under 18 with parental consent generally required, cross-border transfers need adequacy or Commission-adopted safeguards with documented transfer assessments, and DPOs are mandatory for public authorities and large-scale monitoring or sensitive processing. Enforcement is nascent — the Commission is still standing up its data protection function — but the compliance clock has started for organisations processing Gambian data.

summary: Georgia's Law on Personal Data Protection (No. 3144, adopted 14 June 2023) replaced the 2011 law, with its main provisions in force since 1 March 2024. It is closely modelled on the GDPR and was a deliverable of Georgia's EU association agenda. The law applies to processing in Georgia and introduces GDPR-familiar machinery: legal bases, data subject rights, records of processing, mandatory DPOs for public institutions and organisations doing large-scale or sensitive-data processing, direct-marketing rules, and video surveillance provisions.

Breaches likely to cause significant harm must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours. Cross-border transfers follow an adequacy-based model, with safeguards or authority permission required for other destinations. Administrative fines are modest by European standards — GEL 1,000 to 10,000 depending on the offence, adjusted for the violator's turnover and aggravating or mitigating circumstances — though reputational and inspection risk is real, as the regulator has been an active inspector since 2024.

The big 2026 development is institutional: under a December 2025 amendment, the independent Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS) was abolished on 2 March 2026 and its supervisory functions transferred to the State Audit Office, as part of a broader restructuring that also dissolved the Anti-Corruption Bureau. The government frames the SAO as a constitutionally independent home for the function; critics see a weakening of dedicated data protection oversight. Organisations should watch how SAO enforcement practice develops and update any references to the PDPS in their documentation.

summary: Germany applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG), enacted in 2017 and effective alongside the GDPR on 25 May 2018. The BDSG uses the GDPR's opening clauses extensively: it lowers the DPO-appointment threshold (mandatory once 20 or more people regularly process personal data), adds detailed rules on employee data processing (§26 BDSG), credit scoring, and video surveillance, and each of the 16 Länder has its own state data protection law for its public sector.

Supervision is uniquely decentralised. The federal BfDI oversees federal public bodies and telecommunications/postal providers, while 17 independent state authorities (Landesdatenschutzbehörden) supervise the private sector and state public bodies — so a company's lead German regulator depends on where it is established. Coordination happens through the Datenschutzkonferenz (DSK), which issues joint guidance. German authorities are prolific enforcers, with landmark fines against H&M (€35m) and others, and German courts see heavy GDPR damages litigation.

For businesses, the German specifics that matter most are the low DPO threshold, strict works-council and employee-data rules, conservative positions on consent and tracking (reinforced by the TDDDG for cookies), and the need to identify the correct state authority. Enforcement culture is formalistic and complaint-driven, and audits are common.

summary: Ghana was an early African mover on data protection: the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) has been in force since October 2012 and established the Data Protection Commission (DPC), one of the continent's more active regulators. The Act applies to anyone processing personal data using equipment or a controller in Ghana, imposes eight data protection principles broadly modeled on pre-GDPR European law, and gives data subjects rights of access, correction and compensation. Its most distinctive operational feature is mandatory registration: every data controller must register with the DPC and renew every two years, and processing without registration is a criminal offence.

Enforcement is real but modest by modern standards — penalties are criminal fines (capped around GHS 60,000) and imprisonment rather than GDPR-style turnover-based administrative fines, and the Act lacks a fixed breach-notification deadline, a mandatory DPO, and a dedicated cross-border transfer regime. The DPC compensates with sustained registration and compliance campaigns, and in practice pushes larger controllers to designate data protection supervisors.

The framework is on the cusp of a major overhaul: a Data Protection Bill, 2025 would repeal and replace Act 843 with a far more stringent regime — turnover-linked penalties, detailed cross-border transfer rules with data-localization preferences (mandatory localization for children's, biometric, health and national-identity data), parental consent requirements, and rules on automated decision-making. As of mid-2026 the Bill was still being finalized for introduction in Parliament, so Act 843 remains the operative law for any near-term compliance discussion.

summary: As an EU member state, Greece is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented since August 2019 by Law 4624/2019, which implements the member-state derogations and transposes the Law Enforcement Directive. The combined framework applies to any organisation established in Greece and to foreign organisations offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Greece. Law 4624/2019 also carried over rules in areas like employee data processing, which is a well-litigated topic before the Greek regulator.

Greece's notable national choices include setting the digital age of consent at 15 (parental consent required below that for online services), specific conditions for processing employee data, and a EUR 10 million cap on administrative fines against public bodies. Otherwise the standard GDPR machinery applies: 72-hour breach notification, DPOs where Article 37 triggers are met, DPIAs for high-risk processing, and the Chapter V transfer regime.

The Hellenic Data Protection Authority (HDPA), a constitutionally established independent authority based in Athens, is an active enforcer — its fines have ranged from a few thousand euros up to EUR 20 million, targeting telecoms, banks and employers for unlawful employee monitoring, transparency failures and security lapses. Companies operating in Greece should treat HDPA enforcement risk as comparable to other mature EU regulators.

summary: Grenada passed a comprehensive Data Protection Act (No. 1 of 2023), assented on 9 May 2023 and published in the Official Gazette on 10 May 2023 — but the Act is not in force. It commences only on a date appointed by ministerial Order in the Gazette (different dates may be set for different provisions), and no commencement order had been identified as of mid-2026. The recorded status of 'no law' therefore understates progress: Grenada has a fully enacted modern statute sitting dormant, awaiting political action that could come at any time.

The Act establishes seven data protection principles, lawful bases for processing personal and sensitive data, data subject rights including access and rectification, and an Information Commission empowered to investigate complaints, issue enforcement notices and impose penalties. Sanctions are criminal-style: individuals face up to EC$50,000/3 years on summary conviction or EC$100,000/5 years on indictment, while bodies corporate face up to EC$250,000 (summary) or EC$500,000 (indictable), with accountability extending to senior corporate officers. The bill attracted some local controversy during passage over its scope and press-freedom implications.

Local commentary during 2025 (e.g. warnings to financial institutions to prepare for banking data protection demands) suggests commencement is anticipated. Businesses in Grenada should treat this as a compliance runway: map data flows and governance now so that commencement — which requires only a minister's signature — does not catch them unprepared.

summary: Guatemala still has no comprehensive data protection law in force as of mid-2026. The main vehicle is Bill (Iniciativa) No. 6105, the Personal Data Protection Law, introduced on 23 June 2022. In 2025-2026 it advanced through the Congressional Transparency and Probity Commission and was returned to the plenary of Congress, where it must survive three debates (or a two-thirds 'national emergency' vote for fast-track approval). A newer initiative, No. 6572 on personal data protection and digital rights, has also been presented, so the legislative picture is active but unresolved.

In the meantime, privacy protection rests on partial instruments: the 1985 Constitution (which recognizes privacy and habeas data-style guarantees), and Decree 57-2008, the Law on Access to Public Information, which contains limited rules on sensitive personal data held by public bodies. There is no supervisory authority, no registration or breach-notification regime, and no general private-sector obligations.

For businesses, this means Guatemala is currently a low-regulation environment on paper, but multinational groups typically apply regional (GDPR-style) standards voluntarily. Anyone processing Guatemalan data should track Bill 6105/6572, since an approved law would introduce a supervisory authority and GDPR-inspired obligations.

summary: Guinea regulates personal data through Law No. L/2016/037/AN of 28 July 2016, a hybrid statute whose first part deals with cybercrime and whose second part sets out a personal data protection regime. The data protection portion follows the francophone West African model inspired by the ECOWAS Supplementary Act: processing rests on express prior consent or another legitimate basis, data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and most processing is subject to a prior declaration filed with the supervisory authority before it can begin.

The law's biggest practical weakness is institutional. It provides for the creation of a national data protection authority, but a decade after enactment that authority has still not been effectively established, so the declaration regime, complaint handling and sanctions exist largely on paper. Businesses operating in Guinea should treat the substantive principles (consent, purpose limitation, security) as binding law, while recognising that active administrative supervision and enforcement are minimal in practice.

There is no EU adequacy decision, no operational registration portal, and little published enforcement history. Companies typically benchmark against the text of the 2016 law plus the ECOWAS framework, and monitor for the eventual establishment of the authority and implementing decrees.

summary: Guinea-Bissau has no data protection law and no supervisory authority, making it one of the very few ECOWAS member states without such legislation. It also lacks adjacent frameworks such as comprehensive cybercrime or electronic transactions laws, so there is no operative statutory regime governing how organisations collect or process personal data.

The main protections are constitutional and regional: the Constitution enshrines rights to privacy and, by extension, personal data protection, but without implementing legislation the direct applicability of these rights to data processing disputes is unclear. As an ECOWAS member, Guinea-Bissau is also covered in principle by the 2010 ECOWAS Supplementary Act on Personal Data Protection, though this has no practical domestic enforcement machinery.

Drafting of a national data protection law has reportedly been initiated, aiming to regulate processing and establish a legal and institutional framework, but as of mid-2026 no bill has advanced to enactment. Political instability — including the 2025 coup — makes near-term legislative progress uncertain. Businesses operating there typically apply regional or contractual standards voluntarily.

summary: Guyana's Data Protection Act 2023 (No. 18 of 2023) was passed by the National Assembly on 9 August 2023 and assented by President Ali on 16 August 2023 — but the recorded status of 'in force' is wrong: the commencement order has never been issued, so the Act is not operational. The gap became conspicuous in 2026 when the Digital Identity Card Act was commenced (31 March 2026) even though the Commissioner who administers the digital ID registry is a creature of the still-dormant Data Protection Act; the EU Election Observer Mission and local commentators have pressed the government to activate the law, citing misuse of 'cash grant' personal data.

Institutional groundwork is finally moving: Aneal Giddings, a former senior GECOM official, was appointed Data Protection Commissioner in February 2026, and as of May 2026 was formally establishing the Data Protection Office. The Act itself is a modern, broadly GDPR-aligned framework: data protection principles, controller/processor duties, security obligations, 72-hour breach notification to the Commissioner (and notification of data subjects), cross-border transfer conditions based on adequacy and safeguards, and tiered administrative penalties reaching GYD 20 million for serious violations, with parallel criminal offences.

Practical read: treat Guyana as 'imminent regime'. A Commissioner exists and the state is building enforcement infrastructure around the digital ID rollout, so commencement could come quickly; organisations in Guyana's fast-growing economy should map processing and prepare breach and transfer procedures now.

summary: Haiti has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on general sources: the 1987 Constitution's protections for private life and correspondence, civil-law personality rights, and scattered sectoral provisions. Commentators on Haitian digital law describe a significant regulatory vacuum, with services like the national identification card and digitized exam results collecting personal data without a dedicated statutory framework, fueling identity-theft concerns.

Legislative attempts have stalled. A draft law instituting the single national identification card and addressing personal data protection was published by the government (circa 2017) but never enacted, and a draft personal data protection law text has circulated via the civil-service reform office (OMRH) without advancing. Industry association AHTIC has publicly called for data protection legislation. DLA Piper's country guide (updated January 2025) confirms there is still no dedicated data protection entity and references only a ministerial arrêté touching on personal data rules rather than any comprehensive law.

Given the ongoing political and security crisis, near-term enactment is unlikely. Organizations handling Haitian personal data should apply contractual safeguards and best practices voluntarily, as there is no local registration, breach notification, or transfer regime to comply with.

summary: Honduras has no comprehensive data protection law in force as of mid-2026. A Law for the Protection of Confidential Personal Data (Ley de Protección de Datos Personales) has been under discussion in the National Congress for years — an earlier bill stalled around 2018, and a renewed project has seen Congress approve initial chapters, but the law as a whole remains unenacted. If passed, it would create Honduras's first dedicated data protection authority and a rights framework for data subjects.

Existing protection is fragmentary: the 1982 Constitution recognizes the right to privacy and habeas data (a constitutional action allowing individuals to access and correct data held about them), and the Transparency and Access to Public Information Law (Decree 170-2006) imposes confidentiality duties on public bodies handling personal data. The Institute for Access to Public Information (IAIP) oversees that transparency regime but is not a general data protection regulator.

Practically, there is no registration, breach-notification, or fining regime for private-sector data processing. Companies operating in Honduras should monitor the congressional bill, since chapter-by-chapter approval suggests eventual passage, and should rely on constitutional habeas data and sectoral confidentiality rules in the interim.

summary: Hungary applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by Act CXII of 2011 on Informational Self-Determination and Freedom of Information (the "Infotv."), which was amended in 2018 to fit the GDPR. Distinctively, the Infotv. extends GDPR-style rules to processing outside the GDPR's scope (such as law enforcement and national security files) and contains notable provisions on deceased persons' data, allowing relatives to exercise rights for up to five years after death. Hungary kept the GDPR's default digital consent age of 16.

The regulator is the NAIH, which enforces both the GDPR and the domestic act and also supervises freedom of information. It is an assertive enforcer with a steady stream of fines — including high-profile cases on AI-based voice analysis, unlawful CCTV and data-subject-rights failures — and it drew international attention with its ex officio investigation into Pegasus spyware use. Fines follow the GDPR ceilings of EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover.

Compliance is standard GDPR: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, DPOs where triggered, and Chapter V transfer mechanics, plus Hungarian specifics on employee monitoring (regulated in the Labour Code) and deceased persons' data.

summary: Iceland applies the EU GDPR through the EEA Agreement, implemented and supplemented nationally by Act No. 90/2018 on Data Protection and the Processing of Personal Data, in force since 15 July 2018. For practical purposes Iceland operates like an EU member state on data protection: the same principles, data subject rights, breach rules and penalty ceilings apply to any organisation processing personal data of people in Iceland.

The national law makes use of GDPR opening clauses in a few distinctive ways — notably, it extends protection to data about deceased persons for five years after death, and sets the digital age of consent at 13. Maximum administrative fines are expressed in local currency at up to ISK 2.4 billion or 4% of worldwide turnover.

The supervisory authority is Persónuvernd, an active, independent regulator based in Reykjavík that handles a high volume of complaints for a small jurisdiction and participates in EU-level cooperation as an EEA authority. Because Iceland is inside the EEA/GDPR zone, personal data flows freely between Iceland and the EU without any adequacy mechanism being needed.

summary: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) is the country's first comprehensive data protection law, applying to digital personal data processed in India and to processing abroad connected with offering goods or services to individuals in India. After a two-year wait, the DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025, bringing the regime to life: the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI) was established the same day as a fully-online adjudicatory body, and MeitY notified a phased commencement calendar (14 November 2025, 14 November 2026, and 14 May 2027 tranches).

The Act is deliberately leaner than the GDPR: it uses 'Data Fiduciary'/'Data Principal' terminology, recognizes only consent and defined 'legitimate uses' as bases, and layers heavier duties (DPO, annual DPIAs and audits, algorithmic due diligence) on government-designated Significant Data Fiduciaries. Distinctive features include verifiable parental consent for everyone under 18 with a ban on tracking and targeted ads at children, registered Consent Managers as an interoperability layer, and a negative-list (blacklist) approach to cross-border transfers rather than adequacy assessments.

Enforcement reality: the Board exists and breach reporting machinery is being stood up, but the substantive obligations and the penalty regime — headline fines up to INR 250 crore per incident — bite fully from mid-May 2027. Businesses operating in India should use the 2025–2027 runway to build consent, breach-response and children's-data workflows now.

summary: Indonesia's Law No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection (UU PDP) is Southeast Asia's largest GDPR-style framework, consolidating more than 30 fragmented sectoral rules into one law that covers both digital and physical processing by public and private controllers, with extraterritorial reach where processing has legal effects in Indonesia. Its two-year transition period ended on 17 October 2024, so obligations are fully binding.

The law's centerpiece obligations are familiar: lawful bases with explicit consent as the default, data subject rights, mandatory breach notification within 3×24 hours, DPO appointment above thresholds, and cross-border transfers conditioned on equivalent protection or safeguards. Administrative fines can reach 2% of annual revenue, and the law also carries criminal offences for unlawfully obtaining, disclosing, or falsifying personal data — at least 23 criminal cases have already invoked it.

The main gap is institutional: the independent supervisory agency (Lembaga PDP) the law mandates has still not been established. A draft Presidential Regulation was published in February 2026 and awaits presidential approval, with an operational target during 2026. In the meantime, enforcement sits with Komdigi's Directorate General of Digital Space Supervision, and the key implementing government regulation is still being finalized — so administrative fining practice remains untested.

summary: Iran has no comprehensive data protection law in force; a draft has been in progress for years without enactment. The best-known text is the Draft Bill on Protection of Data and Privacy in Cyberspace (2018), prepared by the ICT Ministry, and successor drafts of a Personal Data Protection and Safeguarding Bill have circulated through government and parliament (Majlis) since, but none has become law as of mid-2026. No national data protection authority exists.

In the meantime, privacy protection is scattered across sectoral and general instruments: the Electronic Commerce Law (2004) contains consent-based rules for personal data in electronic transactions; the Computer/Cyber Crimes Act (2011) criminalizes publishing another person's images, recordings or personal and family secrets without consent (61 days to 6 months' imprisonment or IRR 1-10 million fines); the non-binding Charter on Citizens' Rights (2016), the Law on Publication of and Access to Data (2010), the Constitution and Sharia principles round out the picture.

For businesses, there are no registration, DPO, breach notification or cross-border transfer requirements — but data practices intersect with Iran's heavy internet controls, localization pressures via the National Information Network agenda, and criminal exposure for wrongful disclosure. Sanctions considerations dominate any practical engagement. The draft bill's timetable remains unclear, and its passage would likely still leave enforcement in the hands of state bodies rather than an independent DPA.

summary: Iraq has no comprehensive data protection law in force and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on fragmented sources: the 2005 Constitution guarantees personal privacy (Article 17) and confidentiality of communications (Article 40), the Penal Code contains general privacy-related offences (e.g., disclosure of secrets), and the Civil Code offers general tort remedies. Sector-specific obligations exist mainly through Communications and Media Commission (CMC) directives and licensing conditions for telecom operators and digital platforms.

A draft Personal Data Protection Law — reportedly introduced to the Council of Representatives around 2021 and envisaging a national data protection authority — has been mentioned by several legal trackers, but it has not advanced visibly, has not been enacted, and reliable official documentation of its status is scarce. A long-running draft Cybercrime (Information Technology Crimes) Law and a draft Right to Information Act (2023) have drawn criticism for potential restrictions on expression and privacy rather than protections.

In practice, businesses processing Iraqi personal data face no registration, DPO, breach notification or transfer requirements under a general data law, but should observe CMC telecom/platform rules, contractual confidentiality, and Penal Code exposure for wrongful disclosure. The regulatory direction remains uncertain amid Iraq's broader legislative gridlock.

summary: Ireland is governed directly by the GDPR, given further effect by the Data Protection Act 2018, in force since 25 May 2018. The Act establishes the Data Protection Commission (DPC), sets the digital age of consent at 16 — the highest level the GDPR permits — and adds child-specific protections: a specific right to erasure for data collected from children online, and criminal offences for companies that process children's data for direct marketing, profiling or micro-targeting.

Ireland's outsized importance comes from the GDPR's one-stop-shop: because Meta, Google, Apple, TikTok, Microsoft/LinkedIn and many other multinationals have their EU headquarters in Dublin, the DPC is lead supervisory authority for much of Big Tech's European processing. Its decisions — often shaped by EDPB dispute-resolution — include some of the largest fines in GDPR history, most famously the €1.2 billion Meta transfer decision in 2023, giving the DPC an enforcement docket of global significance despite long-standing criticism from privacy advocates about pace.

For ordinary organisations, compliance in Ireland is standard GDPR compliance — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs and Chapter V transfer safeguards — with particular care around children's data given the 16-year consent threshold and the DPC's Children's Fundamentals guidance.

summary: Israel's Protection of Privacy Law (PPL) dates to 1981, but Amendment 13 — passed in August 2024 and effective 14 August 2025 — transformed it into a modern, GDPR-influenced regime. The amendment modernized core definitions (personal information, sensitive ('specially sensitive') data, processing), introduced mandatory Data Protection Officers for public bodies, data brokers and large-scale/sensitive-data processors, drastically narrowed the old database registration duty, and armed the Privacy Protection Authority (PPA) with real teeth: administrative inquiries, cease-and-desist orders, and formula-based monetary penalties that can reach millions of shekels for large or sensitive databases.

The framework is complemented by the Privacy Protection (Information Security) Regulations 2017 — which impose tiered security requirements and require immediate reporting of serious security incidents to the PPA — and the 2001 Transfer Regulations plus dedicated 2023 regulations governing data received from the EEA. Israel has held an EU adequacy decision since 2011, reconfirmed by the European Commission in January 2024, so EU-Israel data flows remain free, though civil society has pressed the Commission to revisit the decision.

Enforcement reality is shifting fast: pre-Amendment 13 the PPA relied mainly on audits and modest sanctions; since August 2025 it operates with substantially expanded penalty and supervision powers, and individuals can claim statutory damages without proving harm. Companies handling Israeli data should confirm DPO applicability, security tiering, and breach playbooks against the new regime.

summary: Italy applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by the Personal Data Protection Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003, the "Codice Privacy"), which was overhauled by Legislative Decree 101/2018 to align with the GDPR rather than being repealed. The Code sets the digital consent age at 14, keeps criminal offences for unlawful processing and fraudulent acquisition of data, preserves sector rules (employment, health, journalism, electronic communications), and keeps in force many of the Garante's pre-GDPR general authorisations and codes of conduct.

The regulator, the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, is one of Europe's most assertive: it issued Europe's early landmark actions on generative AI (temporary limitation and fine against OpenAI/ChatGPT), fined Clearview AI, runs aggressive cookie and telemarketing enforcement, and treats age verification as a substantive compliance duty for online and AI services. Telemarketing abuses have drawn some of Italy's largest fines.

Compliance is standard GDPR — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, DPOs where triggered — with Italian distinctives: the age-14 rule, criminal exposure under the Code, strict Garante positions on employee monitoring and metadata (e.g. email retention), and detailed telemarketing/cookie rules.

summary: Jamaica's Data Protection Act, 2020 (DPA) is a comprehensive, GDPR-inspired law passed in June 2020 and fully in effect since 1 December 2023 after a two-year transition. It applies to public and private data controllers established in Jamaica or using equipment there, and is built around eight data protection standards covering fair and lawful processing, purpose limitation, accuracy, retention, data subject rights, security, and restrictions on overseas transfers.

The Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC), operational since December 2021, supervises the regime. Distinctive features include mandatory registration of data controllers with the OIC (with annual fees), a strict 72-hour breach notification duty, and criminal — not just administrative — liability: individuals face fines up to JMD 5 million and up to 10 years' imprisonment, while corporate offenders can be fined up to 4% of annual gross worldwide turnover, one of the toughest sanction ceilings in the Caribbean.

Enforcement is in its early phase: the OIC has focused on registration drives, guidance, and breach-response supervision since the compliance deadline. Organizations doing business with Jamaica should confirm registration status, appoint a data protection officer where required, and have a tested 72-hour breach-response process.

summary: Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI), originally enacted in 2003 and substantially rewritten by amendments effective April 2022, is a mature, comprehensive privacy law applying to virtually all private-sector businesses handling personal information, with extraterritorial reach over foreign operators serving people in Japan. It is enforced by the independent Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). Japan holds an EU adequacy decision (2019, reaffirmed after review), operating a mutual adequacy arrangement with the EU — a distinctive 'data free flow with trust' posture Japan has championed globally.

The APPI is less prescriptive than the GDPR: no DPO mandate, no general registration, and a purpose-notification model rather than strict legal bases. Its sharpest teeth are the mandatory breach regime (report qualifying incidents to the PPC promptly, with a final report within 30 days, or 60 for malicious acts, and notify affected individuals), rules on third-party provision (traceability records and the opt-out filing system), pseudonymized/anonymized data categories, and cross-border transfer conditions requiring consent, an adequate destination, or safeguards plus detailed disclosures about the destination country's regime. Corporate fines reach JPY 100 million for order violations and database theft.

A significant amendment was enacted in 2026 as part of the APPI's triennial review: it introduces protections for minors under 16, extends improper-use and improper-acquisition prohibitions to 'contactable personally referable information,' and moves individual breach notification to a more risk-based approach; provisions will phase in over the coming years. The PPC enforces mainly through guidance, investigations and binding orders rather than headline fines, but compliance expectations — especially around breach reporting and transfers — are taken seriously by Japanese business.

summary: Jordan's Personal Data Protection Law No. 24 of 2023 is the kingdom's first comprehensive data protection statute. Published in September 2023, it became effective on 17 March 2024, with a one-year transition ending 17 March 2025 — so all controllers and processors, public and private, are now expected to be fully compliant. The law is broadly GDPR-inspired: consent-centric processing, data subject rights (access, correction, erasure, objection), sensitive-data safeguards, and accountability duties.

Institutionally, Jordan chose a ministry-anchored model rather than a fully independent regulator: a Personal Data Protection Council chaired by the Minister of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship sets policy, while a Data Protection Unit within MoDEE handles complaints, compliance inspections, and a registry of controllers and processors. DPO appointment is mandatory for a fairly wide band of organizations — those whose core activities involve personal or sensitive data, data of incapacitated persons, financial data, or transfers abroad.

Enforcement combines administrative fines (JOD 1,000–10,000, plus daily fines for continuing breaches capped at 3% of annual revenue) with judicial penalties that double for repeat offenses. Cross-border transfers are restrictive on paper — generally requiring an adequate level of protection or informed consent. As the regime only recently exited its transition period, published enforcement practice is still limited; expect the Unit's early activity to focus on registration and complaint handling.

summary: Kazakhstan's Law No. 94-V 'On Personal Data and Their Protection', in force since 2013 and amended repeatedly, is a consent-centric regime: collecting and processing personal data generally requires the data subject's consent unless a statutory exception applies. It applies to state bodies and private 'owners' and 'operators' of personal data databases, and is supplemented by ministerial rules on collection and processing. The authorized state body is the Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation and Aerospace Industry, which gained explicit oversight and enforcement functions through amendments in the early 2020s.

Kazakhstan's most distinctive features are data localization and, since 1 July 2024, rapid breach reporting. Personal data of Kazakh citizens must be stored in databases physically located in Kazakhstan — copies may be transferred abroad, but the primary database stays onshore. Cross-border transfers are permitted to jurisdictions ensuring adequate protection or with consent and other statutory grounds. Data breaches must now be reported to the Ministry within one working day of discovery, one of the shortest deadlines anywhere.

Enforcement historically leaned on the Administrative Offences Code, whose MCI-indexed fines are modest by international standards, with criminal liability reserved for serious unlawful collection or dissemination; regulators have signalled tightening oversight amid a string of high-profile leaks. There is no general registration or licensing of controllers, but organisations must designate a person responsible for data processing, adopt internal documentation, and destroy or depersonalise data once the purpose is fulfilled.

summary: Kiribati has moved decisively from having no data protection framework to actively legislating one. The Data Protection Bill 2025 — a first for the country — passed its first reading unanimously in the Maneaba ni Maungatabu (Parliament) on 1 April 2025 and was expected to proceed to a second reading in a subsequent session. The Bill would be cited as the Data Protection Act 2025 and commences on a date the Minister appoints by notice; final passage and commencement could not be verified from official sources as of August 2026, so it is recorded here as a bill in progress.

The Bill is a modern, GDPR-influenced but deliberately lightweight framework tailored to a small island state. It applies to processing within Kiribati and extraterritorially where goods/services are offered to, or behaviour monitored of, people in Kiribati. Enforcement sits with the existing Digital Transformation Office (established under the Digital Government Act 2023) rather than a new standalone regulator, and the Office can investigate complaints, issue compliance notices, and impose administrative penalties up to AUD 20,000 (Kiribati uses the Australian dollar). A distinctive feature is the phased application: most domestic entities that are not 'controllers of major importance' (10,000+ data subjects) are exempt until the second anniversary of commencement, giving small local businesses a long runway.

Until the Bill is enacted and commenced, practical protections rest on the Cybercrime Act 2021 (confidentiality and computer-misuse offences) and sectoral confidentiality rules. Professionals should watch for the second-reading vote and the ministerial commencement notice, and note the two-year grace period for smaller controllers once in force.

summary: Kuwait has no comprehensive data protection statute passed by parliament. Its main framework is regulator-issued: the Data Privacy Protection Regulation (DPPR), first adopted by the Communication and Information Technology Regulatory Authority (CITRA) as Resolution No. 42 of 2021 and replaced by Resolution No. 26 of 2024, effective 19 February 2024. The Governance Atlas entry citing 'DPPR (2021)' should be updated to the 2024 regulation. The DPPR applies to CITRA-licensed telecom and ICT service providers — a category broad enough in practice to cover operators of networks, websites, smart applications and cloud services in Kuwait — regardless of where the data is processed.

Substantively the DPPR is GDPR-flavored: transparency and accessible privacy policies, informed consent before collection, purpose limitation, security and encryption requirements, data subject rights to access, rectify, delete and withdraw consent, notice before transferring personal data outside Kuwait, and a strikingly short 24-hour breach notification window to CITRA. Sanctions run through CITRA's licensing regime — fines and suspension of operating licenses — rather than a standalone administrative fine schedule.

For meetings, the key framing is that Kuwait's regime is sectoral secondary legislation, not an economy-wide statute: entities outside CITRA licensing largely face only general confidentiality and constitutional privacy principles. Enforcement by CITRA is opaque, with little published penalty practice. Watch for movement toward a full national data protection law as neighbors (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Jordan) have enacted theirs.

summary: Kyrgyzstan's Law No. 58 'On Personal Information' of 14 April 2008 was one of Central Asia's earliest data protection statutes, and it has been significantly modernized by amendments in 2017, 2021 and 2022. It regulates collection, processing and protection of personal data by public and private 'holders', built on consent or another lawful basis, purpose limitation, and data subject rights of access and correction.

A dedicated regulator — the State Agency for Personal Data Protection under the Cabinet of Ministers — was established in December 2021, giving the law an enforcement arm it previously lacked. Its flagship mechanism is mandatory registration: holders of personal data arrays must register with the Agency via a three-stage online process launched in November 2022 (currently workable mainly for local entities). There is no formal DPO requirement, though a responsible person must be identified at registration, and there is no general breach notification duty to the Agency — but data subjects must be told within a week if their data was passed to third parties without consent.

Cross-border transfers rely on international treaties ensuring adequate protection, data subject consent, or narrow statutory grounds. Enforcement is young and penalties are modest; the practical compliance question for companies operating in Kyrgyzstan is completing registration and consent documentation as the new Agency ramps up activity.

summary: Laos regulates personal data primarily through the Law on Electronic Data Protection No. 25/NA, adopted 12 May 2017. It governs the collection, processing, storage, use and transfer of data in electronic form — covering both 'general' and 'specific' (sensitive-type) data — and applies to state bodies, private entities and foreign businesses handling electronic data of Lao residents within Laos or via local infrastructure. It requires consent for collection and disclosure, imposes basic security and confidentiality duties, and gives individuals rights to access, correct and request deletion of their data.

The Ministry of Technology and Communications (MTC) is the responsible authority, but there is no dedicated, independent data protection regulator, no DPO or registration regime, and no GDPR-style breach notification deadline. The law is materially narrower than modern comprehensive statutes — it applies only to electronic data, its obligations are framed at a high level, and implementing practice is thin. Related provisions also appear in the Law on Prevention and Combating Cyber Crime and the Penal Code.

Enforcement is minimal in practice: penalties are modest (secondary sources report fines in the LAK 5–50 million range, with suspension of activities and criminal liability for serious cases), and no significant public enforcement actions are documented. Businesses should treat Laos as a consent-and-confidentiality jurisdiction with low regulatory activity but growing government interest in cyber and data controls.

summary: Latvia applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the Personal Data Processing Law, which entered into force on 5 July 2018 — making Latvia the first Baltic state to adopt GDPR-aligned national legislation, replacing its 2000 Personal Data Protection Law. The national law sets out the powers and procedures of the supervisory authority, lowers the age of children's consent for information society services to 13, and regulates specific contexts such as processing for journalistic, academic and official-purposes.

The supervisory authority is the Data State Inspectorate (Datu valsts inspekcija, DVI), operating since 2001 and now functioning as Latvia's GDPR authority under Cabinet of Ministers supervision. The DVI handles complaints, conducts inspections, and issues fines; enforcement activity and fine levels have historically been modest compared with larger EU authorities, but the DVI is active in guidance, DPO certification exams, and cross-border cooperation through the EDPB.

Compliance in Latvia is standard GDPR practice — lawful basis, Latvian-language transparency notices, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs for high-risk processing. The main local particularities are the 13-year consent age for online services and national rules on personal identity codes and journalistic processing.

summary: Lebanon's Law No. 81 of 10 October 2018 on Electronic Transactions and Personal Data (in effect since 31 March 2019) is the country's first legislation addressing personal data, but it is a hybrid statute — most of it concerns e-transactions, e-signatures, e-commerce and cybercrime, with one section devoted to personal data. It defines processing broadly (collection, recording, storage, transmission, deletion) and establishes basic conditions of lawful, consented processing along with data subject rights of access and correction.

Its most distinctive — and dated — feature is a licensing model: rather than an independent regulator, oversight sits with the Ministry of Economy and Trade, which issues permits and licenses for personal data processing where required. In practice broad exemptions (consent-based processing, employers processing employee data, businesses processing customer data for legitimate operations, public authorities, non-profits, schools) mean most routine processing needs no permit. The law contains no DPO requirement, no breach notification duty, and no dedicated cross-border transfer regime.

Enforcement has been minimal amid Lebanon's economic and institutional crisis, and civil society (notably SMEX) has criticized the law as falling well short of GDPR-style protection. Companies handling Lebanese data face light formal obligations, but should watch for reform proposals and note that sectoral rules (banking secrecy, telecom) can impose stricter duties than Law 81 itself.

summary: Lesotho enacted one of Southern Africa's earliest data protection statutes — the Data Protection Act, published in the Government Gazette on 22 February 2012 — making the recorded status of an in-force law correct. The Act applies to automated and manual processing, sets out familiar principles (minimality, purpose specification, security safeguards), treats children's data as sensitive personal information requiring parental consent, requires controllers to notify the Data Protection Commission before processing, and mandates breach notification 'as soon as reasonably possible' to the Commission and affected individuals. Its transfer rules are distinctive for privileging SADC member states that have transposed equivalent protections.

The fatal weakness is institutional: the Data Protection Commission the Act establishes has never been appointed. Fourteen years on there is no commissioner, no registration machinery, no guidance and no enforcement — local practitioners describe the law as having 'no teeth'. Even if constituted, the Commission's powers are weaker than modern peers; notably, it cannot impose administrative fines, leaving only limited criminal penalties.

Practically, organisations in Lesotho face a technically enforceable statute with zero supervisory activity, and reform advocates are pressing for a modernised law and an operational authority. Compliance is prudent (courts could still apply the Act, and enforcement could reach past conduct once a Commission exists), but there is no regulator to register with today.

summary: Liberia's status has moved from 'no law, no bill' to an active legislative process. The country still has no specific data protection law, but a draft Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act — 'An Act for the Collection, Processing, Transmission, Storage, Protection, and Use of Personal Information in Liberia' — was developed by the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications with Internews support under the EU-funded Liberia Media Empowerment Project.

Over 50 stakeholders from government, media, civil society, education and the diplomatic corps validated the draft in Monrovia in December 2024, and after Law Reform Commission review, President Joseph Boakai submitted the bill to the Legislature, where the House of Representatives took up review during 2025. As of August 2026 there is no confirmation of enactment, so the bill remains in progress.

In the interim, protections are fragmentary: constitutional privacy guarantees, plus sectoral instruments (telecommunications and cybercrime-related provisions). A 2025 UN review highlighted the gaps in Liberia's online rights framework, adding international pressure to complete the legislation. Organisations handling Liberian data should track the bill, which would create the country's first structured framework and supervisory arrangements for personal data.

summary: Libya has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on scattered provisions: the Constitutional Declaration protects private life (Article 12) and the confidentiality of correspondence and communications (Article 13), and the 1953 Penal Code contains general protections for private correspondence and the home.

The closest things to modern data rules are sectoral and digital-economy statutes. Law No. 6/2022 on Electronic Transactions and Law No. 5/2022 on Combating Cybercrime introduce some data-handling and security obligations, though it remains unclear how far the Electronic Transactions Law binds private entities. In June 2025 the Central Bank of Libya issued Circular No. 18, a 'Data Protection System and Executive Regulation' creating data protection requirements specifically for the banking and financial sector — the most concrete data protection instrument in the country to date.

There is no supervisory authority for personal data; the National Information Security & Safety Authority (NISSA) handles information security rather than privacy enforcement. Organizations operating in Libya face contractual and sectoral obligations (especially in banking) rather than a general compliance regime, and no comprehensive bill was identified as pending as of mid-2026.

summary: Liechtenstein applies the GDPR through its EEA membership, supplemented by the national Data Protection Act (Datenschutzgesetz, DSG) enacted on 4 October 2018. The DSG implements the member-state opening clauses: it retains the GDPR's default age of 16 for children's consent to information-society services, regulates processing by public authorities, and sets national criminal and procedural provisions. Being a microstate deeply integrated with both the EEA and Switzerland, Liechtenstein is a common jurisdiction for financial-sector data flows.

Supervision belongs to the Datenschutzstelle, a small but functional independent authority that participates in the European Data Protection Board alongside EU regulators. Enforcement volume is naturally low given the country's size — guidance and complaint-handling dominate over headline fines — but the full GDPR sanction regime of up to EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover applies to private entities.

Compliance obligations mirror the GDPR everywhere in the EEA: lawful basis, transparency, data subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, DPO designation where triggered, and Chapter V transfer tools for exports outside the EEA. Its banking and fiduciary industries add sectoral secrecy duties on top.

summary: Lithuania applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the amended Law on Legal Protection of Personal Data (original law No I-1374 of 1996, comprehensively amended by Law No XIII-1426 of 30 June 2018, in force 16 July 2018). The national law lowers the children's online consent age to 14, sets rules for processing personal identification codes, employee data and video surveillance, caps fines on public authorities, and splits supervision between two bodies.

The main regulator is the State Data Protection Inspectorate (VDAI) in Vilnius, which handles complaints, breach notifications, inspections and fines; the Inspector of Journalist Ethics supervises processing for journalistic purposes. The VDAI issued one of the earlier notable GDPR fines (against payment company MisterTango in 2019) and remains active in inspections and guidance, though fine levels are generally moderate.

Compliance is standard GDPR practice with Lithuanian specifics: Lithuanian-language transparency, the 14-year consent age, restrictions on using the personal identification code as a public identifier, and prior-notice rules for workplace monitoring. Cross-border work runs through the EDPB one-stop-shop with the VDAI as national contact.

summary: Luxembourg applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by the Act of 1 August 2018 on the organisation of the National Data Protection Commission (CNPD) and the general data protection framework, effective 20 August 2018, which repealed the 2002 data protection law. A companion Act of the same date transposes the Law Enforcement Directive for criminal-justice processing. The national act keeps derogations light: it retains the GDPR default consent age of 16, adds conditions for employee monitoring and processing for scientific research, and exempts the State and municipalities from administrative fines.

The CNPD, based in Belvaux, supervises a market dense with banks, funds, and EU-headquartered tech companies — Amazon's EU headquarters made the CNPD its lead authority, producing the landmark €746 million fine against Amazon in 2021, one of the largest GDPR penalties ever issued (contested in the Luxembourg courts). Day-to-day, the CNPD favours audits, thematic investigations (CCTV, geolocation, DPO function) and published guidance.

Compliance is standard GDPR practice with local nuances around bank secrecy, employee monitoring rules under the Labour Code (works-council involvement and CNPD-relevant notice duties), and the practical significance of Luxembourg as lead supervisory authority for multinationals established there.

summary: Madagascar's Law No. 2014-038, adopted in December 2014 and promulgated on 9 January 2015, is a pre-GDPR, French-inspired data protection statute. It applies to automated and manual processing carried out wholly or partly on Malagasy territory, imposes classic principles (lawfulness, purpose limitation, accuracy, security, confidentiality) and relies on prior formalities — declarations and authorisations — rather than the accountability model of newer laws. It has no general breach-notification duty and limited children-specific rules.

The big development is institutional: for nearly a decade the law was a dead letter because its supervisor, the Commission Malagasy de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CMIL), did not exist. The CMIL was created by Decree 2023-1541 (December 2023), its members were sworn in before the Supreme Court on 4 August 2025, and it adopted its procedures manual in December 2025. It joined the francophone association of DPAs (AFAPDP) as a full member in November 2025, with operationalisation support from the OIF and AFAPDP.

Enforcement reality: the CMIL declares itself fully operational and holds both regulatory and sanctioning powers under the 2014 law, but it is a brand-new regulator with no enforcement track record, and the underlying statute is dated relative to GDPR-era peers. Expect guidance, registration mechanics and possibly a modernised law to develop over the next few years.
madagascar.xborder: Transfers permitted only to countries ensuring adequate protection, subject to CMIL oversight

summary: Malawi's Data Protection Act, 2024 was gazetted in February 2024 and came into force on 3 June 2024, replacing the thin data-protection provisions of the Electronic Transactions and Cyber Security Act 2016 with a comprehensive, GDPR-inspired regime. It applies to automated and manual processing by controllers and processors, sets out familiar principles (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security) and grants data subjects rights of access, correction, erasure and objection.

The Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (MACRA) is the designated Data Protection Authority and operates a dedicated portal (dpa.mw). Distinctive features include a tiered registration regime for 'significant' data controllers and processors (those processing data of more than 10,000 subjects or data of national importance), mandatory DPOs for large-scale processing, 72-hour breach notification, and transfer restrictions based on adequacy or safeguards such as binding corporate rules.

Enforcement is young: the framework is in place and MACRA has been standing up registration and guidance, but there is little published enforcement history yet. Penalty exposure under the Act is primarily criminal (fines and imprisonment) rather than GDPR-scale administrative fines.
malawi.xborder: Restricted unless recipient country ensures adequate protection or safeguards (e.g. binding corporate rules) apply

summary: Malaysia's Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709) governs the processing of personal data in commercial transactions and is enforced by the Personal Data Protection Commissioner via the Personal Data Protection Department (JPDP) under the Ministry of Digital. Notably, it does not apply to the federal and state governments or to purely non-commercial processing. The Act rests on seven data protection principles, with certain classes of data users required to register with the Commissioner.

The regime was substantially modernized by the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024, whose phases came into force through 2025: direct obligations on data processors, mandatory data breach notification to the Commissioner within 72 hours (and to individuals where significant harm is likely), mandatory DPO appointment above processing thresholds from 1 June 2025, a new data portability right, biometric data classed as sensitive, and higher penalties — up to RM 1 million and/or three years' imprisonment for breaching the principles.

Cross-border transfers were also overhauled: the old ministerial white-list was abolished on 29 April 2025 in favor of transfers to jurisdictions with substantially similar laws or with an ensured equivalent level of protection, operationalized through Transfer Impact Assessments under the CBPDT Guidelines. With new guidelines, an active registration regime and a modernized toolkit, Malaysian enforcement is expected to sharpen considerably.
malaysia.xborder: White-list abolished — transfers allowed to jurisdictions with substantially similar laws or where equivalent protection is ensured, supported by Transfer Impact Assessments (2025 CBPDT Guidelines)

summary: The Maldives currently has no comprehensive data protection law in force, but the position has moved from 'nothing' to 'bill in progress': in 2026 the Attorney General's Office finalized a government-backed Personal Data Protection Bill, which was submitted to the People's Majlis (sponsored by West Henveiru MP Ali Ibrahim). The bill aims to establish a full legal framework for the collection, processing and use of personal data, define responsibilities of data processors, regulate sensitive data, and control transfers of data to foreign entities.

This follows an earlier Privacy and Personal Data Protection Bill draft released for public consultation in May 2023, which contemplated GDPR-style principles (lawful, fair, transparent processing), data subject rights to access, correct, delete and object, security obligations, breach notification to a new supervisory body, and a Privacy Commissioner with complaint-handling and enforcement powers.

Pending enactment, protections rest on the constitutional right to privacy in the 2008 Constitution and scattered sectoral rules; there is no supervisory authority, registration scheme, breach notification duty or administrative fining regime. Businesses handling Maldivian data should monitor the Majlis process, as the government has signalled a transition period before full compliance is required once the bill passes.

summary: Mali's Law No. 2013-015 of 21 May 2013 on the Protection of Personal Data is a comprehensive statute in the Francophone mold, establishing the legal bases on which personal data may be collected and processed in Mali and protecting privacy as a fundamental right. It was amended by Law No. 2017-070 of December 2017, which adjusted the functioning of the supervisory authority.

The Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (APDP), launched in 2016, is among the more visibly active authorities in the Sahel: it receives declarations and authorization requests, issues warnings, formal notices and injunctions, can withdraw approvals, and can impose monetary fines ranging from XOF 2.5 million to XOF 20 million; criminal sanctions including imprisonment also back the law.

The regime predates GDPR-era concepts, so there is no general DPO mandate or 72-hour breach clock; compliance in practice centers on completing prior formalities with the APDP and responding to its supervision. Mali's political instability has not dissolved the authority, but cross-border and enforcement details should be confirmed with the APDP directly for current practice.

summary: Malta is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly, supplemented by the Data Protection Act (Act XX of 2018, Chapter 586 of the Laws of Malta), in force since 28 May 2018, which repealed the previous Chapter 440 regime. Malta chose the lowest permitted child consent age — 13 — for information society services, and subsidiary legislation under Cap. 586 covers ePrivacy in electronic communications (S.L. 586.01), the Law Enforcement Directive (S.L. 586.08) and sector-specific processing rules.

The supervisory authority is the Information and Data Protection Commissioner (IDPC), appointed under Article 11 of the Act, which enforces both the GDPR and the national Act and also administers freedom-of-information functions. The national Act moderates fines against public authorities and bodies with reduced statutory caps, while private-sector exposure follows the full GDPR maxima of €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover.

Given Malta's outsized iGaming, financial services and remote-services sectors, the IDPC's caseload skews toward complaints about online operators, employee monitoring and direct marketing. Compliance in Malta is standard GDPR compliance, with attention to the age-13 consent threshold and the local subsidiary legislation.

summary: The Marshall Islands still lacks a comprehensive data protection law, but there is a notable new development: the Personal Data Protection Act 2025 (P.L. 2025-43), which commenced on 7 October 2025 and is codified at Title 6, Chapter 4 of the Marshall Islands Revised Code. Crucially, the Act applies only to 'core Government ministries and agencies' of the national government — it does not regulate the private sector, state-owned enterprises, or local governments, and it excludes law enforcement and national security processing.

Within its public-sector scope, the Act sets out data protection principles, designates the Economic Policy, Planning and Statistics Office (EPPSO) as competent authority (with education, coordination and reporting duties rather than fines), establishes a complaints process and a private right of action with remedies, and regulates data sharing among ministries with a safe-harbor mechanism. It is best understood as groundwork for the country's digital ID program; the government has signaled plans for a broader data protection law as that program develops (reportedly by 2028).

For businesses, the practical position is unchanged: no registration, no DPO, no breach notification and no transfer restrictions apply to private-sector processing. Protection otherwise rests on the constitutional right to privacy and fragmented provisions in sectoral statutes such as the Persons with Disabilities Act (2015) and Gender Equality Act (2019). The Marshall Islands holds no EU adequacy decision.

summary: Mauritania enacted Law No. 2017-020 on the Protection of Personal Data on 22 July 2017, a comprehensive statute in the Francophone declaration/authorization tradition establishing lawful-processing principles, data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure) and a supervisory authority. Implementation lagged badly: the decree organizing the Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (APD) was only adopted in February 2022, and its members were sworn in later that year.

The APD is now functioning: it published a 2023–2026 strategic plan framed around bringing Law 2017-020 into effective application, signed a cooperation agreement with Algeria's ANPDP in October 2024, and joined the Global Privacy Assembly in November 2024. However, its enforcement track record is thin, and some secondary sources still describe the law as not yet fully effective in practice — the gap between the statute and day-to-day enforcement is the defining feature of the Mauritanian regime.

Companies operating in Mauritania should expect prior-formalities obligations with the APD and honor core data subject rights, but should verify current APD practice directly, as guidance, penalty practice, and detailed rules (breach notification, transfers, DPO expectations) are not yet well documented publicly.

summary: Mauritius's Data Protection Act 2017 (Act 20 of 2017), in force since early 2018, replaced the 2004 Act specifically to align with the GDPR and modernise one of Africa's oldest data protection regimes. It applies to controllers and processors established in Mauritius or using equipment there, covers the full set of GDPR-style principles and data subject rights, requires 72-hour breach notification to the Data Protection Commissioner, and sets a parental-consent age of 16 for children's data. Mauritius was the first African state to sign and ratify Council of Europe Convention 108 and its modernised 108+ protocol, underlining its position as a regional privacy leader.

Two features stand out for foreign businesses. First, registration is genuinely mandatory: every controller and processor must register with the Data Protection Office and renew its certificate every three years, and processing without registration is a criminal offence. Second, every controller and processor must designate a data protection officer. Cross-border transfers require Commissioner-approved safeguards, explicit consent or another statutory ground.

Enforcement is real but criminal-law flavoured: the Data Protection Office, an established and active regulator, investigates complaints and issues enforcement notices, with offences punishable by fines up to MUR 200,000 and imprisonment up to five years rather than turnover-based administrative fines. Mauritius does not hold an EU adequacy decision, though its Convention 108+ status and GDPR alignment ease practical transfer arrangements.

summary: Mexico replaced its 2010 private-sector data protection law with an entirely new LFPDPPP, published 20 March 2025 and effective 21 March 2025. The rewrite was driven by a constitutional 'organic simplification' reform (December 2024) that dissolved seven autonomous bodies — including INAI, the independent data protection authority operating since 2010. Supervision and enforcement of both the private-sector law and public-sector rules now sit with the executive-branch Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno (SABG).

Substantively the regime remains recognizable: controllers need a privacy notice (aviso de privacidad), a lawful basis with express consent for sensitive and financial data, designated data protection personnel to process ARCO (access, rectification, cancellation, opposition) requests, security measures, and conditions on transfers. Breach notification runs to affected data subjects — there is still no general duty to notify the regulator, though the SABG has signaled that mandatory regulator notification, formal DPO rules, and DPIAs are priorities for further legislation. Fines range from 100 to 320,000 UMA.

The critical governance point for foreign counsel is independence: moving enforcement from an autonomous institute into a government ministry runs counter to international best practice and complicates any future EU adequacy ambitions. Enforcement under the SABG is still ramping up, and implementing regulations for the new law are pending, so practical guidance largely carries over from INAI-era criteria.
