summary: The Federated States of Micronesia has no data protection law in force, but the status has moved from 'nothing' to 'draft in progress': Congressional Bill No. 24-17, which would enact the FSM Personal Data Protection Act of 2025 as a new chapter of Title 16 of the FSM Code, was introduced in the 24th FSM Congress on 17 May 2025 and remains pending as of mid-2026.

The bill is narrow by international standards. It would apply only to core national government departments and agencies that collect, use, store, process, disclose or transfer personal data — it would not bind the four states for purely intrastate activity, nor regulate the private sector. It designates the National Statistics Office as the competent authority, sets out familiar data protection principles (legitimate purpose, minimization, accuracy, retention limits, security, accountability), and creates a private right of action without compensatory damages. If approved, it would take effect 18 months after enactment.

Beyond the bill, only fragments exist: telecommunications confidentiality provisions in Title 21 of the FSM Code, constitutional privacy protections, and a separate Cybersecurity Act 2025 initiative. There is no authority, registration regime, DPO requirement, breach duty or transfer restriction applicable to businesses today.

summary: Moldova is in the final weeks of a generational transition. The framework currently in force is Law No. 133 of 8 July 2011 on Personal Data Protection, a Convention 108/Directive 95/46-era law that requires controllers to register processing operations with the National Center for Personal Data Protection (CNPDP), observe lawfulness and proportionality, and respect data subject rights of access, rectification and objection. Enforcement under it operates through the Contravention Code, with modest fines — a recent published penalty was MDL 6,500 (about EUR 330).

On 25 July 2024 Parliament adopted Law No. 195/2024 on personal data protection, which substantially transposes the GDPR and becomes applicable on 23 August 2026 — this month. It replaces Law 133/2011 with GDPR architecture: accountability duties for controllers and processors, expanded data subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, DPO requirements, a GDPR-style transfer regime, and far heavier sanctions, ending the old registration model. The two-year transition period given to organisations is now effectively over.

Anyone dealing with Moldova today should treat Law 195/2024 as the operative benchmark: EU candidate-country alignment is driving convergence with the GDPR, and the CNPDP is repositioning as a GDPR-style supervisory authority. Moldova does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so transfers from the EU still need safeguards.
moldova.xborder: Free to states with adequate protection; otherwise CNPDP authorisation or specific grounds

summary: Monaco comprehensively overhauled its data protection framework with Law No. 1.565 of 3 December 2024, which repeals and replaces the 1993 law (Law 1.165) and aligns the Principality with the GDPR and Council of Europe Convention 108+. The law has extraterritorial scope modelled on GDPR Article 3: it covers controllers and processors established in Monaco and foreign ones offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Monaco. Sovereign Ordinance No. 11.327 of 10 July 2025 set out the detailed implementing rules, and pre-existing processing benefits from a one-year transitional window.

The former Commission de Contrôle des Informations Nominatives (CCIN) has been replaced by the Autorité de Protection des Données Personnelles (APDP), which has substantially stronger powers, including administrative fines of up to €10 million or 4% of worldwide turnover. The law strengthens data subject rights (information, access, rectification, erasure, portability), introduces DPIAs for high-risk processing, mandatory records of processing, DPO designation for certain categories of organisations, and certification mechanisms.

The shift is from the old prior-formalities culture (declarations and authorisations to the CCIN) to a GDPR-style accountability model. Monaco does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so EEA exporters still need safeguards to send data to Monaco, though the 2024 reform is widely seen as positioning Monaco for a future adequacy bid.

summary: Mongolia's Law on Personal Data Protection was adopted on 17 December 2021 and took effect on 1 May 2022, replacing a 1995-era individual-secrets law. It was passed as part of a package with the Cybersecurity Law, Public Information Transparency Law and Electronic Signature Law, together forming Mongolia's first comprehensive digital-governance framework. The law applies to individuals, legal entities and organisations collecting, processing and using personal data in Mongolia, and is broadly consent-based, with heightened rules for sensitive categories including health, genetic and biometric data.

Distinctively, Mongolia has no dedicated data protection authority: compliance oversight sits with the National Human Rights Commission of Mongolia, while the Ministry of Digital Development and Communications handles digital-security aspects. There is no registration regime and no general DPO mandate. Sanctions are imposed under the general Law on Violations, with fines ranging from roughly MNT 500,000 to MNT 20,000,000 (about USD 150–5,800) depending on the offence.

Enforcement is still maturing — the NHRC's role is closer to a human-rights ombudsman than an inspecting regulator, and practice on issues like breach handling and cross-border transfers (generally consent-based) is thin. Businesses operating in Mongolia should anchor compliance in documented consent, purpose limitation, security measures for sensitive data, and the specific rules on workplace monitoring and CCTV that the law introduced.

summary: Montenegro still operates under its pre-GDPR Personal Data Protection Law of 2008 (Official Gazette 79/08 and 70/09), amended several times since — most recently in July 2024. The law follows the old EU Directive 95/46 model: it applies to controllers processing personal data in Montenegro, requires a legal basis for processing, obliges controllers to register their data filing systems with the supervisory Agency, and channels most enforcement through a misdemeanour-fine regime with maximum penalties of only EUR 20,000 for legal entities.

Supervision sits with the Agency for Personal Data Protection and Free Access to Information (AZLP), which handles both data protection and freedom-of-information. Cross-border transfers to countries lacking adequate protection require the Agency's approval, and there is no general data breach notification duty — hallmarks of the framework's age. Enforcement is real but low-stakes by European standards, and the European Commission has repeatedly flagged that the law is not aligned with the GDPR or the Law Enforcement Directive.

A comprehensive GDPR-aligned replacement law has been in the works for years as part of Montenegro's EU accession (Chapter 23). In March 2026 the Ministry of Interior submitted the draft new Law on Personal Data Protection to the European Commission for review, but as of August 2026 it has not been adopted by Parliament. Anyone doing business in Montenegro should comply with the 2008 law today while preparing for a GDPR-style overhaul in the near term. Note that some secondary trackers incorrectly report a 2023 GDPR-aligned act as already in force — official and law-firm sources confirm the 2008 law remains the one in effect.
montenegro.xborder: Transfers to countries without adequate protection require AZLP approval

summary: Morocco's Law 09-08, promulgated in February 2009, was one of the first comprehensive data protection statutes in North Africa and is closely modeled on the pre-GDPR European Directive 95/46/EC. It applies to public and private controllers processing personal data in Morocco and operates on a prior-formalities model: no processing may begin until the controller has obtained either a declaration receipt or an authorization from the regulator, the CNDP, based in Rabat.

The CNDP is one of Africa's most active data protection authorities. It reviews declarations, handles complaints, conducts audits and issues sanctions, and continues to publish detailed deliberations — including a set of five adopted in November 2025 covering cookies, newsletters, CCTV in healthcare facilities and workplace access control — with a dedicated deliberation on AI processing in preparation as of 2026.

Enforcement relies on criminal-style fines (MAD 10,000–300,000 and up to two years imprisonment for the most serious violations) rather than GDPR-scale administrative penalties. A modernization of Law 09-08 toward closer GDPR alignment has been under study for several years but had not been enacted as of mid-2026, so the 2009 declaration/authorization regime remains the operative framework.

summary: Mozambique still has no dedicated data protection law, so the recorded 'bill in progress' status remains correct — but the bill has advanced materially. The National Institute of Information and Communication Technologies (INTIC) published a draft Personal Data Protection Bill for public consultation in September 2025 and consulted the Council of Europe in October 2025 to align it with international standards. In early 2026 the Council of Ministers approved the Bill, which now awaits debate and approval in the Assembly of the Republic.

The Bill would create Mozambique's first comprehensive regime, including an Autoridade Nacional de Protecção de Dados Pessoais (ANPD) — expected to be built on the existing telecommunications regulator — with powers to investigate complaints, issue regulations and impose sanctions, alongside GDPR-style principles, data subject rights and transfer rules.

Pending enactment, protection rests on the constitutional right to privacy, the Electronic Transactions Law and sectoral confidentiality rules (telecoms, banking, health), none of which amount to a general data protection framework. There is no supervisory authority, registration duty, breach-notification obligation or administrative fine regime today.

summary: Myanmar has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. Privacy-related provisions are scattered across sectoral statutes: the Law Protecting the Privacy and Security of Citizens (2017), the Electronic Transactions Law (2004, amended 2021 to add limited personal-data provisions and offenses), the Telecommunications Law (2013), the Financial Institutions Law (2016), and the Penal Code. None of these creates a general regime of data subject rights, controller obligations, or independent supervision.

The environment has deteriorated since the February 2021 military coup. Key protective provisions of the 2017 privacy law (including warrant requirements for surveillance and searches) were suspended by the State Administration Council, and the junta enacted a sweeping Cybersecurity Law (Law No. 1/2025) on 1 January 2025, effective 30 July 2025. That law regulates digital platform service providers (registration required at 100,000+ users), restricts VPN use, and extends jurisdiction extraterritorially — but it is oriented toward state control and surveillance rather than personal data protection.

For businesses, the practical picture is a legal vacuum on privacy paired with expanding state access to data. Any data handling connected to Myanmar carries political and human-rights risk considerations that outweigh conventional compliance analysis, and there is no realistic prospect of a GDPR-style law under the current administration.

summary: Namibia still has no comprehensive data protection law, so the recorded status of 'bill in progress' remains correct. Government published a Draft Data Protection Bill in 2021, and in August 2025 the Minister of Information and Communication Technology, Emma Theofelus, said the Bill was in its final stage and would be tabled in Parliament around September–October 2025. As of early 2026, however, the Bill had still not been enacted, and reporting through February 2026 confirms no comprehensive law is in force.

The Bill would establish a supervisory authority, data subject rights and controller obligations broadly aligned with international norms; civil society groups (including the Association for Progressive Communications) have criticised later drafts for watering down rights and independence safeguards. It forms part of a wider digital-law package alongside cybercrime legislation and the operationalisation of electronic signatures under the Electronic Transactions Act 2019.

In the meantime, protection rests on Article 13 of the Namibian Constitution (privacy of home, correspondence and communications), common-law privacy actions, and sectoral confidentiality rules in areas like banking and telecommunications. There is no regulator, no registration, no breach-notification duty and no administrative fine regime until the Bill passes.

summary: Nauru has no comprehensive data protection or privacy law, no supervisory authority, and no draft bill that could be verified as of August 2026. The Constitution's Part II (Protection of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms, Articles 3–15) provides general fundamental-rights protection that implicitly supports privacy, but there is no dedicated statutory privacy right or personal-data regime.

Partial, sector-specific protections exist. The Cybercrime Act 2015 criminalises unauthorised access to computers, illegal interception of communications and data interference — addressing data protection only from a confidentiality angle. The Communications and Broadcasting Act 2018 adds safeguards for subscriber information held by telecom providers. The government has signalled interest in modernising cyber and electronic-evidence legislation, which could eventually address data protection more directly, but nothing concrete has been published.

In practice, organisations handling Nauruan personal data face no local registration, breach notification, transfer or DPO requirements; the main exposure is criminal liability for unauthorised access or interception under the Cybercrime Act.

summary: Nepal's Individual Privacy Act, 2075 (in force 18 September 2018) was the country's first dedicated privacy statute, giving effect to the constitutional right to privacy (Article 28 of the 2015 Constitution). Supplemented by the Individual Privacy Regulation 2020 and provisions of the National Civil and Penal Codes, it regulates the collection, retention, analysis, processing and publication of personal information by public authorities and Nepali-incorporated corporate bodies, covering identifiers such as ethnicity, religion, education, biometric data, ID numbers and criminal records.

The Act is privacy-focused rather than a full GDPR-style data protection code: it establishes consent requirements and confidentiality duties, but has no supervisory authority, no registration or DPO requirements, no breach notification regime, and no dedicated cross-border transfer mechanism. Enforcement runs through the courts — violations are criminal offences prosecuted on complaint, punishable by fines up to roughly NPR 30,000 and/or up to three years' imprisonment, alongside compensation claims.

The practical reality is thin enforcement: cases are rare, remedies are individual rather than systemic, and compliance culture is nascent. Businesses processing Nepali data should anchor on documented consent and purpose limitation. Discussion of a modern data protection law and authority continues, but no bill has been enacted.

summary: The Netherlands is governed directly by the EU GDPR, supplemented by the national GDPR Implementation Act (Uitvoeringswet AVG, or UAVG), both effective 25 May 2018. The UAVG fills in the areas where the GDPR leaves member states discretion — for example retaining the default age of 16 for children's online consent and setting rules for processing national identification numbers (BSN), which may only be used where a statute specifically permits it. The framework applies to any organisation established in the Netherlands and to foreign organisations targeting or monitoring people there.

The regulator, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP) in The Hague, is one of Europe's more active authorities. It has issued some of the EU's largest fines — including a €290 million penalty against Uber in 2024 over unlawful transfers of driver data to the US — and publishes extensive Dutch-language guidance on cookies, algorithms and AI. The AP also serves as one of the Netherlands' coordinating regulators for the EU AI Act, making it a key interlocutor for companies deploying automated decision-making.

Practically, Dutch compliance is standard GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs for high-risk processing, and DPO appointment where Art. 37 thresholds are met. The main Dutch-specific traps are strict BSN rules, the AP's assertive position on tracking cookies and legitimate-interest advertising, and active private litigation including collective actions under Dutch class-action law.

summary: New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 (replacing the 1993 Act) governs how 'agencies' — nearly every public body and private organisation, including overseas businesses carrying on business in NZ — handle personal information, structured around 13 Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) covering collection, storage, access, correction, accuracy, retention, use, disclosure and unique identifiers. Distinctive features include a mandatory privacy officer for every agency (a broader requirement than the GDPR's conditional DPO), a principles-based rather than consent-based collection model, mandatory breach notification to the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals when serious harm is likely, and IPP 12 controls on overseas disclosure. New Zealand holds an EU adequacy decision — one of the few Asia-Pacific jurisdictions to do so.

Enforcement is compliance-oriented rather than punitive: the Privacy Commissioner can investigate complaints, issue compliance notices and access directions, but criminal fines max out at NZD 10,000; substantive remedies flow through the Human Rights Review Tribunal, which can award damages for interference with privacy. The regime's teeth are reputational and remedial rather than turnover-based penalties — a frequent law-reform criticism.

The framework is actively evolving through sector codes: the Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, issued 21 July 2025 and in force 3 November 2025, imposes a necessity/proportionality test, mandatory privacy impact assessment, transparency notices and bias assessment (including for Māori and Pacific peoples) on agencies using biometrics, with a grace period for existing users ending 3 August 2026. Health, credit reporting and telecommunications codes similarly modify the IPPs for their sectors.

summary: Nicaragua enacted Law No. 787, the Personal Data Protection Law, on 29 March 2012, with an implementing regulation (Decree 36-2012) issued the same year. On paper it is a habeas-data-style comprehensive law: it protects individuals' informational self-determination, requires consent for processing, grants rights of access, rectification, and cancellation, and mandates that data files be registered with a supervisory body, the Dirección de Protección de Datos Personales (DIPRODAP), which the law places under the Ministry of Finance (MHCP).

The regime's defining feature is that it has never been operationalized: DIPRODAP was never actually established or staffed, the data-file registry required by the law does not function, and no meaningful administrative enforcement has taken place in the fourteen years since enactment. Legal commentators consistently cite the absence of the authority as the law's central weakness — obligations exist in text but complaints have no functioning regulator to receive them, leaving judicial habeas data actions under the Constitution as the practical remedy.

For organizations handling Nicaraguan data, the law still formally applies — consent, purpose limitation, and security duties are on the books — but compliance risk is driven more by reputational and constitutional-litigation exposure than by regulatory action. The broader governance environment also means reform toward an independent, active DPA is unlikely in the near term.

summary: The recorded entry for Niger is out of date: Law No. 2017-28 of 3 May 2017 (as amended in 2019) was repealed and replaced by Law No. 2022-59 of 16 December 2022 on the protection of personal data, itself modified by Law No. 2023-31 of 4 July 2023. Law 2022-59 is now Niger's principal, comprehensive data protection statute, and the country therefore remains in the 'law in force' category — but citations should point to the 2022 Act.

The supervisory authority is the Haute Autorité de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (HAPDP). The 2022 Act introduced modern elements including a mandatory breach-notification duty: under Article 83, controllers must inform the HAPDP without delay upon becoming aware of a breach, and must inform data subjects as soon as possible where there is high risk to their rights and freedoms. Notably, the law contains no DPO appointment requirement. Non-compliance with obligations, including breach notification, is backed by criminal penalties (imprisonment and fines) under Article 98.

Enforcement reality is shaped by Niger's post-July 2023 political situation: the HAPDP has continued operating, with commentary through 2024 describing an authority balancing awareness-raising against control activity. Practical enforcement remains light, and detailed transfer and penalty specifics under the 2022-59/2023-31 framework are not well documented in accessible public sources.

summary: North Korea (DPRK) has no data protection or privacy law in any recognizable sense, and no supervisory authority. The state operates one of the world's most pervasive surveillance systems: personal information is collected and used by the state for control purposes, and there are no independent bodies, judicial remedies or legal mechanisms through which citizens could challenge the handling of their data.

The legislation that does touch information is oriented toward state control rather than individual rights — for example, the Law on Protection of State Secrets adopted in 2023, which criminalizes leakage of classified information and further restricts citizens' access to and dissemination of information. Enforcement is carried out by the Ministry of State Security without oversight, with penalties that can include imprisonment, forced labour or execution.

For any organization, the question of DPRK data compliance is academic: foreign businesses do not process North Korean personal data under local law, and comprehensive international sanctions bar most commercial activity. There is no constitutional or statutory privacy protection with practical effect, no DPO, registration, breach or transfer rules, and no realistic prospect of data protection legislation.

summary: North Macedonia's Law on Personal Data Protection (Official Gazette No. 42/2020, amended by 294/21) took effect on 24 February 2020 and is a close transposition of the EU GDPR, adopted as part of the country's EU accession agenda. After an 18-month transition, it has been fully applicable since August 2021. It covers controllers and processors on Macedonian territory and adopts GDPR concepts wholesale: legal bases, data subject rights, records of processing, DPIAs, and privacy by design.

The old general database registration requirement from the 2005 law was scrapped — the Agency's Central Registry survives only for high-risk databases, which controllers must notify. DPOs are mandatory for public bodies and for organisations doing large-scale systematic monitoring or extensive special-category processing. Breaches must be reported to the Agency within 72 hours unless unlikely to pose a risk to individuals.

Enforcement is handled by the Agency for Personal Data Protection (AZLP) in Skopje, an independent state body with inspection and sanctioning powers. Fines mirror the GDPR's turnover-based logic — up to 4% of a company's total annual income of the preceding financial year, with additional personal fines of EUR 300–500 for responsible officers. In practice the Agency is active on complaints and inspections, though headline fines remain far smaller than in EU member states.

summary: Norway applies the full text of the EU GDPR through the EEA Agreement, incorporated by the Personal Data Act of 15 June 2018 (personopplysningsloven), which entered into force on 20 July 2018. The Act fills the gaps the GDPR leaves to national law — for example on the digital age of consent (13), employment-related processing and exemptions — but the substantive regime is the GDPR itself, applying to any organisation established in Norway or targeting people there.

The supervisory authority, Datatilsynet, is one of Europe's more assertive enforcers relative to market size, with a record that includes the landmark Grindr fine over unlawful sharing of user data with advertisers, and firm positions on tracking, cloud services and workplace monitoring. Because Norway sits outside the EU institutional framework, Datatilsynet participates in the European Data Protection Board without voting rights, but applies EDPB guidance in practice.

As an EEA state inside the GDPR zone, Norway needs no EU adequacy decision — personal data flows freely between Norway and EU member states, and transfers out of the EEA follow the standard GDPR Chapter V toolkit.

summary: Oman's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL), issued by Royal Decree 6/2022, is the Sultanate's first comprehensive data protection statute and one of the stricter regimes in the Gulf: it is consent-centric, requiring a lawful basis (usually express consent) for most processing, and layering a government permit requirement on top for sensitive categories such as health, genetic and biometric data. It applies to controllers and processors handling personal data in Oman, with the Ministry of Transport, Communications and Information Technology (MTCIT) acting as regulator rather than a standalone data protection authority.

Executive Regulations issued in 2024 (Ministerial Decision 34/2024) fleshed out the law — DPO appointment, breach notification within 72 hours, permits for sensitive data, and data subject rights to access, correction, deletion and portability. The transition period ended on 5 February 2026, so the PDPL is now fully enforceable and MTCIT has moved into an active supervisory role.

Enforcement reality is two-track: relatively modest administrative fines (up to OMR 2,000 per violation, plus permit suspension or cancellation), but severe criminal penalties — up to OMR 500,000 — for serious breaches such as unlawful cross-border transfer or processing of sensitive data without a permit. Businesses operating in Oman should treat the permit and consent requirements as the distinctive compliance risks.

summary: Pakistan still has no comprehensive data protection law. A Personal Data Protection Bill has been through repeated drafts since 2018 (2020, 2021, a Cabinet-approved 'final draft' in May 2023, and a further Personal Data Protection Act 2025 draft), but as of mid-2026 none has been passed by the National Assembly and Senate. The drafts are GDPR-inspired — consent-based processing, data subject rights, 72-hour breach notification, and a proposed National Commission for Personal Data Protection (NCPDP) as regulator — but have drawn sustained criticism for broad state exemptions and data localization requirements for 'critical' personal data.

In the meantime, partial protections apply. Article 14 of the Constitution recognizes the dignity and privacy of the home; the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA) 2016 — amended most recently in January 2025 — criminalizes unauthorized access to data and certain misuse of personal information; and sectoral rules (banking, telecom licensing by the PTA) impose confidentiality duties. None of this gives individuals general rights of access, correction or erasure, and there is no supervisory authority for personal data.

The practical read for businesses: no registration, DPO, or breach filing obligations exist today, but the direction of travel is toward a strict regime with localization and a powerful new Commission. The 2025 PECA amendments also signal a state-security-heavy approach to digital regulation, which is the central tension delaying the bill.

summary: Palau has no comprehensive data protection or privacy law, no data protection authority, and no general obligations on companies handling personal data. Privacy protection rests on the constitutional right against unreasonable search and invasion of privacy, plus scattered sectoral confidentiality rules (e.g., for government records and the digital residency program's cybersecurity regulations issued by the Ministry of Finance).

Recent legislative activity has focused on security and online harms rather than data protection proper. A 2024 law criminalized the non-consensual distribution of sensitive and intimate images, creating criminal penalties and civil remedies. In October 2025 the Senate unanimously passed Senate Bill No. 12-9 (the Cybersecurity Act), Palau's first comprehensive national cybersecurity framework, which moved to the House of Delegates — but it is a security statute, not a GDPR-style privacy law.

Some low-quality online sources refer to a 'Palau Privacy Act 2019', but this could not be verified against any official Palauan source and should not be relied on. For a professional audience the practical position is: no registration, no DPO, no breach notification and no transfer restrictions apply, and contractual protections are the main tool when handling Palauan personal data.

summary: Panama's Law No. 81 of 26 March 2019 on Personal Data Protection is a GDPR-influenced comprehensive law that entered into force on 29 March 2021 and is fleshed out by Executive Decree 285 of 2021. It applies to databases located in Panama or whose controller is established there, sets out processing principles (loyalty, purpose limitation, proportionality, security), and grants data subjects ARCO-style rights of access, rectification, cancellation, opposition, and portability.

The regulator is ANTAI, the National Authority for Transparency and Access to Information, which handles complaints (including through its online portal), investigates violations, and sanctions offenders. Breaches must be reported to ANTAI without undue delay and at the latest within 72 hours, with affected individuals notified where risk is high. Fines are modest by global standards — US$1,000 to US$10,000 for grave infractions — but very grave infractions can result in suspension or permanent closure of the offending database or activity, and ANTAI has publicly imposed data protection sanctions. Minors' data requires verified parental or guardian authorization, and cross-border transfers depend on ANTAI-recognized adequacy or appropriate safeguards.

Compared with GDPR, Panama's regime is lighter-touch: no mandatory DPO, no general registration, and low monetary ceilings, but the 72-hour breach rule and transfer restrictions mean multinationals typically fold Panama into their regional GDPR-style compliance programs. ANTAI has been increasingly active with awareness campaigns and enforcement since 2022.

summary: Papua New Guinea has no comprehensive data protection law in force. The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) completed the National Data Governance and Data Protection Policy 2024, which sets out principles and commits the government to a regulatory framework addressing data breaches, privacy violations and data misuse — but this is policy, not statute, and no dedicated Data Protection Bill had been tabled in Parliament as of August 2026. Describing PNG as 'bill in progress' therefore slightly overstates the position; it is more accurately at the policy-to-drafting stage.

Legislative energy has instead gone into the digital identity agenda: following the National Digital ID Policy (2025), DICT introduced a proposed Digital Identity and Verifiable Credentials Bill to underpin the SevisPass digital ID, SevisWallet and consent-based data exchange, with rollout targeted for 2026. That bill embeds some consent and data-handling safeguards but is not a general privacy law. In the meantime, protections rest on the constitutional right to privacy (s 49 of the Constitution), the Cybercrime Code Act 2016, and sectoral confidentiality rules.

For businesses, there is currently no registration, breach notification or transfer regime to comply with, and no supervisory authority. The practical risk horizon is the pace at which the 2024 policy is converted into a bill — organisations building data systems for the PNG market should track DICT announcements closely.

summary: Paraguay's status has changed: the bill previously tracked has become law. Law No. 7593/2025, promulgated on 27 November 2025, is the country's first comprehensive data protection statute — the biggest privacy shift in its legislative history. It replaces a patchwork that previously regulated only credit data (Law 6534/2020) with a broad, GDPR-inspired framework covering public and private sector processing of personal data.

The law creates the Agencia Nacional de Protección de Datos Personales (ANPDP) as a decentralized unit of MITIC with functional autonomy and exclusive regulatory, supervisory and sanctioning powers. It establishes data protection principles and data subject rights, heightened protection for sensitive data and minors (parental consent below 16; joint consent for adolescents' sensitive data), breach notification duties, and a tiered sanctions regime topping out at 10,000 minimum daily wages for violations involving children's sensitive data.

Enforcement reality: the framework becomes fully enforceable over a two-year adaptation period (roughly to late 2027), and the ANPDP and implementing regulations are still being stood up as of mid-2026. Businesses are in the compliance-preparation window now. Paraguay holds no EU adequacy decision.

summary: Peru has had a comprehensive, GDPR-influenced data protection law since 2011 — Law No. 29733 — but the regime was substantially modernized by a new implementing Regulation (Supreme Decree 016-2024-JUS), published 30 November 2024 and in force since 30 March 2025. The law applies to public and private entities processing personal data in Peru and, under the new Regulation, extends extraterritorially to foreign companies that offer goods or services to people in Peru or monitor their behavior; such companies must appoint a local representative.

The framework is distinctive in the region for its mandatory registration of 'data banks' with the RNPDP and its consent-centric model: consent must be free, prior, express and informed. The 2024 Regulation added GDPR-style machinery — a 48-hour breach notification duty, revenue-threshold-based data protection officer requirements, and security measures aligned with ISO/IEC 27001.

Enforcement is handled by the ANPD, a directorate within the Ministry of Justice and Human Rights rather than a fully independent agency. It is an active regulator by regional standards, regularly fining companies for unregistered data banks, unlawful marketing and security failures, with penalties reaching 100 UIT for the most serious infringements. Peru does not hold an EU adequacy decision.
peru.xborder: Cross-border flows require an adequate level of protection or contractual guarantees and must be declared to the ANPD

summary: The Philippines' Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173) is one of Asia's older comprehensive privacy laws, modeled largely on EU-style principles of transparency, legitimate purpose and proportionality. It covers personal information controllers (PICs) and processors (PIPs) in both the private and public sectors, with extraterritorial reach where equipment in the Philippines is used or where Philippine residents' data is processed. The National Privacy Commission (NPC) administers the law through Implementing Rules and Regulations and a steady stream of circulars and advisories.

Distinctive features include a genuinely enforced registration regime (annually renewable NPC registration of processing systems), mandatory DPO appointment for all covered organizations, and a strict 72-hour dual notification duty — to the NPC and affected individuals — for breaches involving sensitive personal information likely to cause serious harm. Since NPC Circular 2022-01, the Commission can impose administrative fines scaled to annual gross income (0.25%–3% per infraction, capped at PHP 5 million per act), on top of the DPA's criminal penalties, which include imprisonment.

Enforcement reality is active: the NPC investigates complaints and breaches, orders corrective measures, and publicizes decisions, making the Philippines one of the more operationally mature regimes in Southeast Asia despite the relatively modest fine cap.
philippines.xborder: Accountability model — the controller remains responsible for data transferred abroad and must use contracts or other reasonable means; no adequacy whitelist

summary: Poland is governed by the EU GDPR, supplemented by the Act of 10 May 2018 on the Protection of Personal Data, which took effect on 25 May 2018 and replaced the 1997 act. The 2018 Act contains few substantive derogations from the GDPR: its main role is establishing the supervisory authority (UODO, replacing the former GIODO), setting procedural rules for inspections and administrative proceedings, capping fines on public bodies at PLN 100,000, and retaining the GDPR default age of 16 for children's online consent. A companion 'sectoral implementation' act of 2019 amended over 160 other statutes, including significant employer rules on employee monitoring and recruitment data.

The President of UODO is appointed by the Sejm for a four-year term and runs an active enforcement programme: annual inspection plans, published decisions, and fines against both private companies and public institutions. Decisions can be appealed to the administrative courts, which have overturned several UODO fines, so enforcement is genuinely contested.

In practice, compliance in Poland is standard GDPR work — lawful basis, transparency in Polish, 72-hour breach reporting, DPIAs against UODO's published high-risk list — with local specifics around employee monitoring notice requirements and the obligation to notify DPO appointments to UODO electronically.
poland.xborder: Free within EU/EEA; outside via adequacy decision, SCCs or BCRs (GDPR Ch. V)

summary: Portugal applies the GDPR directly, executed nationally by Law No. 58/2019 of 8 August. The national law sets the digital consent age at 13 — the lowest the GDPR permits — and requires that parental consent for younger children be collected through secure authentication means such as the Citizen's Card. It also contains Portuguese specifics on employee data, health data, deceased persons' data, and video surveillance, and structures fines into national bands within GDPR ceilings.

Supervision belongs to the CNPD (Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados). A notable quirk: shortly after Law 58/2019 passed, the CNPD publicly deliberated that it would disapply several of its provisions it considered incompatible with the GDPR's primacy — so practitioners rely on the GDPR text over the national law where they conflict. The law also allowed public entities a temporary waiver from fines, reflecting a historically softer enforcement posture toward the public sector.

Enforcement has grown steadily, with the CNPD issuing fines on video surveillance, municipalities and data-subject-rights failures, and intervening prominently on international transfers (notably ordering suspension of transfers in the Census 2021 Cloudflare case). Day-to-day compliance is standard GDPR with the age-13 rule and secure parental authentication as Portuguese distinctives.
portugal.xborder: Free flow within EU/EEA; GDPR Chapter V tools (adequacy, SCCs, BCRs) for third countries

summary: Qatar's Law No. 13 of 2016 on Personal Data Privacy Protection (PDPPL) was the first standalone national data protection law in the GCC. In force since 2017, it applies to personal data processed electronically by public and private entities in Qatar (the QFC free zone has its own separate regime). The law rests on principles of transparency, fairness and human dignity, requires consent or another lawful basis, and grants rights of access, correction and erasure.

Administration and enforcement now sit with the National Data Privacy Office (NDPO) within the National Cyber Governance and Assurance Affairs (NCGAA) division of the National Cyber Security Agency (NCSA). The NDPO has issued a substantial set of executive guidelines fleshing out the law — including a 72-hour breach notification expectation, a required 'Personal Data Management System' (incorporating DPIAs and records of processing), permits for sensitive-data processing, and penalty methodology. Distinctively, the PDPPL contains explicit protections for children online, requiring guardian consent and controls on websites directed at minors.

Enforcement has begun in earnest: the NDPO issued compliance rulings against an ICT company in December 2024 and an e-commerce company in March 2025, ordering strengthened administrative and technical safeguards. Fines can reach QAR 5 million, so companies processing Qatari data should align with the NDPO's guideline suite rather than the bare 2016 text.
qatar.xborder: Transfers permitted unless they violate the law or are likely to cause serious harm to data subjects

summary: Romania is an EU member state where the GDPR applies directly, supplemented by Law No. 190/2018 (in force 31 July 2018). The national law adds conditions for processing national identification numbers (CNP), genetic, biometric and health data, workplace monitoring rules, and a distinctive lighter-touch regime for public authorities: ANSPDCP first issues a warning and a remediation plan, and fines on public bodies are capped at RON 200,000.

The framework also includes Law No. 102/2005 establishing the supervisory authority, Law No. 363/2018 transposing the Law Enforcement Directive, and Law No. 506/2004 on ePrivacy in electronic communications. The authority, ANSPDCP, is an autonomous body based in Bucharest that issues secondary regulations on DPIAs, breach reporting and certification.

Workplace monitoring is a notable Romanian specificity: employee monitoring via electronic means or CCTV requires a legitimate-interest justification, prior consultation, and is only allowed if less intrusive methods have not proven effective. Enforcement is regular though fines are typically modest compared with Western European authorities.
romania.xborder: Free within EEA; outside via adequacy, SCCs or other GDPR Chapter V safeguards

summary: Russia's Federal Law No. 152-FZ 'On Personal Data', enacted in 2006, is a comprehensive consent-centric regime that has been amended repeatedly and now anchors one of the world's most restrictive data governance systems. It applies to any 'operator' processing personal data of Russian citizens, and its most distinctive features are mandatory data localization (databases with Russians' personal data must be located in Russia — a rule tightened from 1 July 2025 to cover processors as well), mandatory notification of Roskomnadzor before processing begins, and a separate prior notification before any cross-border transfer, with transfers to some jurisdictions subject to restriction.

Enforcement has hardened sharply since 2022. Breaches must be reported to Roskomnadzor within 24 hours (with a 72-hour detailed follow-up). Federal Law 420-FZ, in force since 30 May 2025, introduced turnover-based fines: data leaks now attract fines of RUB 3–15 million depending on the number of affected individuals, and repeat leak violations can cost up to 3% of annual turnover, capped at RUB 500 million. Parallel Federal Law 421-FZ created criminal liability — up to four years' imprisonment — for illegal collection, use or transfer of personal data, with harsher sentences involving minors' or biometric data.

Roskomnadzor is an assertive regulator with website-blocking powers (LinkedIn has been blocked since 2016 over localization). Russia holds no EU adequacy decision, so GDPR-covered transfers into Russia require safeguards, while outbound compliance for foreign companies serving Russian users is dominated by localization, notification and consent formalities.
russia.xborder: Prior notification to Roskomnadzor before any cross-border transfer; transfers to certain countries can be restricted; strict localization — Russian citizens' data must be stored and processed on servers in Russia

summary: Rwanda's Law No. 058/2021 on the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy (in force since 15 October 2021, with a two-year transition that ended 15 October 2023) is one of Africa's most GDPR-aligned and operationally serious regimes. It applies to controllers and processors in Rwanda and to those abroad processing data of people in Rwanda. Supervision sits with the Data Protection and Privacy Office of the National Cyber Security Authority (NCSA), which runs an active registration system, publishes guidance, and issued standard contractual clauses for transfers in February 2024.

Several features are stricter than the GDPR: breaches must be notified to the NCSA within 48 hours (not 72); registration as a controller or processor is mandatory; a DPO is required for sensitive or large-scale processing; children under 16 need parental consent; and cross-border transfers require NCSA authorization with proven safeguards, consent, or a narrow necessity exception — layered on top of a national policy preference that data be hosted in Rwanda unless approved otherwise. Sanctions combine administrative fines (up to RWF 5 million or 1% of global turnover) with criminal penalties that can reach 5% of turnover and imprisonment.

Enforcement reality: the NCSA is regarded as one of the more capable regulators in the region, registration campaigns have had firm deadlines, and Rwanda's positioning as a digital/financial hub (Kigali International Financial Centre) gives compliance genuine commercial weight. Foreign companies serving Rwandan users should assume the law applies extraterritorially and that registration and transfer approvals will be checked.
rwanda.xborder: NCSA authorization with safeguards (SCCs issued 2024), data-subject consent, or necessity exceptions; storage outside Rwanda needs approval

summary: Samoa has no comprehensive data protection or privacy law and no data protection authority. Several AI-generated legal content sites assert that Samoa has a 'Privacy Act 2013' enforced by an 'Office of the Privacy Commissioner'; no official Samoan government or authoritative international source corroborates this, and it should be treated as unverified and likely erroneous. Actual protections are fragmentary: confidentiality obligations on telecommunications providers under the Telecommunications Act 2005, computer-misuse and privacy-adjacent offences in the Crimes Act 2013, and data safeguards embedded in the National Digital Identification Act 2024 governing the new digital ID system.

Policy momentum is building. The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology's National Communications & ICT Policy 2025–2030 and National Cybersecurity Strategy 2025/26–2030/31 bring connectivity, digital ID, responsible data use and cybersecurity under one framework, and the Ministry has stated it is proposing new legislation to address current gaps including data protection, alongside a national data governance framework for the public sector.

Until such legislation materialises, organisations handling Samoan personal data face no registration, breach notification, DPO or transfer requirements; the main legal exposures are telecom confidentiality duties, digital-ID-specific rules, and criminal provisions in the Crimes Act.

summary: San Marino's Law No. 171 of 21 December 2018 is a comprehensive data protection statute closely modelled on the GDPR — it reproduces the Regulation's principles, lawful bases, data subject rights, accountability obligations and breach-notification regime. A consolidated text incorporating amendments through 2023 is published by the Great and General Council and by the supervisory authority.

The law established an independent supervisory authority, the Autorità Garante per la Protezione dei Dati Personali, a collegial body of three members supported by an office. It holds investigative, corrective, authorisation and advisory powers, including the distinctive ability to grant an infringer a deadline of up to six months to come into compliance before or alongside sanctions (Article 73). Controllers must notify personal data breaches presenting risk to individuals without undue delay and, where possible, within 72 hours.

Despite its GDPR-inspired framework, San Marino does not hold an EU adequacy decision, so EEA organisations transferring data to San Marino still need Chapter V safeguards. Enforcement activity is modest and mostly guidance-oriented, consistent with the microstate's size.

summary: São Tomé & Príncipe enacted Law No. 03/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data as its general data protection framework. The law is closely modeled on the EU's former Data Protection Directive (95/46/EC) and Portugal's Act 67/98, so its architecture will feel familiar to anyone who worked with pre-GDPR European law: consent or another legal ground for processing, prior notification to the regulator (with authorization for sensitive data), data quality principles, and adequacy-based rules for international transfers.

The supervisory authority, the Agência Nacional de Protecção de Dados Pessoais (ANPDP), is a genuine bright spot for a small island state: it is operational and relatively active, issuing authorisations, resolutions and opinions, operating under the National Assembly as an independent administrative entity, and participating in regional networks (NADPA and the francophone AFAPDP). Entities must generally obtain data-subject consent and give prior notice to the ANPDP before collecting and processing personal data.

Because the law predates the GDPR, it lacks modern features — there is no general breach-notification duty, no DPO requirement, and no turnover-based fines — and detailed English-language documentation of penalty levels is sparse. For most international businesses exposure is limited, but anyone processing Santomean data at scale (telecoms, banking, the growing digital-government program) should file notifications with the ANPDP and track possible modernization of the 2016 framework.

summary: Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL) — issued by Royal Decree M/19 in September 2021 and substantially amended in 2023 — is the Kingdom's first comprehensive data protection law. It entered into force on 14 September 2023 with a one-year grace period that ended in September 2024. It applies to any processing of personal data of individuals residing in Saudi Arabia, including by entities outside the Kingdom, and is supplemented by Implementing Regulations and separate Data Transfer Regulations.

The regime is GDPR-influenced but distinctive: controllers must register on SDAIA's National Data Governance Platform, appoint DPOs in defined high-risk cases, notify breaches to SDAIA within 72 hours, and run risk assessments before cross-border transfers. Criminal liability attaches to unlawful disclosure of sensitive data (up to two years' imprisonment) — a notable departure from purely administrative regimes.

Enforcement is real and accelerating: SDAIA, the competent authority since September 2023, had issued roughly 48 enforcement decisions by early 2026, with failure to honor data subject rights and inadequate security controls among the most commonly cited findings. Companies serving the Saudi market should treat PDPL compliance as an active supervisory risk, not a paper exercise.

summary: Senegal was one of Africa's data protection pioneers: Law No. 2008-12 of 25 January 2008 established a comprehensive regime and created the Commission de Protection des Données Personnelles (CDP), one of the continent's first operational supervisory authorities. The law follows the pre-GDPR French/CNIL model — built around declarations and prior authorisations to the regulator rather than accountability tools like DPOs and breach notification.

Controllers must declare most processing to the CDP and obtain prior authorisation for sensitive categories such as biometric and genetic data, criminal records and national ID numbers. There is no mandatory breach-notification duty and DPO appointment is discretionary, which makes the regime feel dated next to newer African laws. Cross-border transfers are permitted only to countries offering 'sufficient protection', assessed by the CDP.

A modernising replacement bill — addressing biometrics, big data, AI and a strengthened authority — has been in preparation since 2019 under the Digital Senegal strategy, with a finalisation workshop held by the CDP and the digital ministry in October 2024, but it had not been adopted as of mid-2026, so the 2008 law remains in force. The CDP is active in awareness-raising and issues regular deliberations, though monetary enforcement has historically been light.

summary: Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection (ZZPL), published in Official Gazette No. 87/2018 and applicable since August 2019, is closely modelled on the GDPR and unusually also incorporates the EU Law Enforcement Directive in the same statute. It brings GDPR-style principles, data subject rights, accountability tools (records, DPIAs, DPOs), 72-hour breach notification and extraterritorial reach over foreign controllers targeting people in Serbia. Serbia set the child consent age for information society services at 15.

The supervisory authority is the Poverenik — the Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection — a well-established independent body that also handles freedom of information. The law's biggest weakness is its misdemeanour-based sanctions: fines are capped at RSD 2 million (roughly €17,000), far below GDPR levels, which limits deterrence even as inspection activity increases.

Reform is underway: the Government adopted a Personal Data Protection Strategy 2023–2030, and in January 2025 a working group began drafting ZZPL amendments to cover gaps such as cookies, video surveillance, biometrics and AI. As of August 2026 the 2018 law remains in force and the amendment timeline is uncertain. Serbia does not hold an EU adequacy decision; cross-border transfers are free to Convention 108 parties and listed adequate countries, with safeguards or Commissioner approval otherwise.

summary: Seychelles' Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 24 of 2023) was gazetted and entered into force on 22 December 2023, replacing the Data Protection Act 2003 — a law that had been enacted but never brought into practical operation. The new Act is a modern, GDPR-influenced framework covering data controllers and processors, with duties around lawful processing, retention, security, cross-border transfers and the appointment of data protection officers for organisations of sufficient size or processing risk.

Supervision sits with the Information Commission, which also handles access to information; it is empowered to conduct audits and investigations and to impose administrative fines. Controllers must notify the Commission within 72 hours of discovering a breach that may put data subjects' rights and freedoms at risk, and children's data (under 18) may only be processed with parental or guardian consent.

All controllers and processors were given an 18-month transition from 22 December 2023, which expired in June 2025 — so the Act is now fully applicable. Enforcement history is still short, and no EU adequacy decision exists; businesses should track Information Commission guidance as its data protection practice develops.

summary: Sierra Leone still has no comprehensive data protection law, but the legislative process is well advanced. The Ministry of Information and Civic Education completed the final national validation of the Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill, 2025 in November 2025, after nationwide consultations involving Parliament, local councils, security agencies, the Electoral Commission, civil society, media, academia and the private sector.

In April 2026, Cabinet approved the country's first National Data Protection Policy and authorized drafting and enactment of a combined Data Protection and Right to Access Information Act — a distinctive design that would merge data protection and access-to-information functions into a single strengthened authority (building on the existing Right to Access Information Commission). The Ministry has been directed to work with the Attorney-General's office to finalize and table the Bill in Parliament.

As of August 2026 the Bill has not been enacted. The forthcoming law is expected to impose stricter protocols on banks, mobile network operators and government agencies over citizens' financial, digital, health and tax records, and to align Sierra Leone with international data standards for trade. In the meantime, protections rest on constitutional privacy rights and sectoral rules such as the Cyber Security and Crime Act, 2021.

summary: Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (PDPA) is the baseline data protection law for the private sector (public agencies are governed by separate government instructions). It is a consent-based, accountability-oriented regime administered by the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), and was significantly modernized by 2020 amendments that added mandatory breach notification, an expanded deemed-consent and legitimate-interests framework, data portability provisions, and a tougher penalty regime effective 1 October 2022.

Every organization, regardless of size, must appoint a Data Protection Officer, and there is no registration requirement — compliance is demonstrated through accountability practices rather than filings. Breaches causing (or likely to cause) significant harm, or affecting 500 or more people, must be reported to the PDPC as soon as practicable and no later than three calendar days after the organization assesses the breach as notifiable. Cross-border transfers require the recipient to be bound to a comparable standard of protection, with APEC CBPR/PRP certifications recognized — reflecting Singapore's interoperability-first approach.

Enforcement is mature and well documented: the PDPC publishes decisions regularly, and maximum financial penalties now reach the higher of SGD 1 million or 10% of annual Singapore turnover. The PDPC also issues detailed advisory guidelines, including 2024 guidance on children's personal data that anchors 13 as the practical age from which minors may consent for themselves.

summary: Slovakia applies the EU GDPR directly, supplemented by Act No. 18/2018 Coll. on the Protection of Personal Data, adopted 29 November 2017 and effective 25 May 2018. Unusually, the Act restates much of the GDPR's text verbatim in Slovak law (to cover processing outside the GDPR's scope and transpose the Law Enforcement Directive), while adding national derogations: it keeps the children's online consent age at 16, regulates processing of birth numbers and employee data disclosure, and sets procedural rules for the supervisory authority.

The Office for Personal Data Protection of the Slovak Republic (Úrad na ochranu osobných údajov SR) in Bratislava supervises compliance, conducts inspections under an annual plan, handles complaints, and issues decisions and methodological guidance. Enforcement is steady but fines are typically modest — usually in the thousands to tens of thousands of euros — with an emphasis on corrective measures.

Compliance is standard GDPR practice with Slovak specifics: transparency in Slovak, the 16-year consent age, restrictions on using the national birth number as an identifier, and a statutory rule allowing employers to disclose limited employee contact data. Because Act 18/2018 duplicates GDPR text, practitioners must track which provisions apply directly under the Regulation versus the national Act.

summary: Slovenia is an EU member state, so the GDPR has applied directly since May 2018. However, Slovenia was famously the last EU country to pass a national GDPR implementing act: the Personal Data Protection Act (ZVOP-2) was adopted in December 2022 and entered into force on 26 January 2023. Until then, the Information Commissioner could not impose GDPR administrative fines because Slovenia lacked the domestic procedural machinery; full and systematic enforcement has only been possible since ZVOP-2 took effect.

ZVOP-2 supplements the GDPR with national specifics: a consent age of 15 for children in information society services, detailed data-security duties including traceability logs for certain processing, rules on video surveillance and biometrics, and localised fine provisions enforced through the fast-track misdemeanour procedure. The Information Commissioner (IP-RS) is a well-regarded, active authority that also handles freedom-of-information matters.

For anyone doing business in Slovenia, compliance is essentially GDPR compliance plus the ZVOP-2 national add-ons. Enforcement has stepped up markedly since 2023, with the IP-RS now conducting audits and imposing fines directly.

summary: Solomon Islands has no data protection law in force, but drafting is genuinely underway. UNCTAD is supporting the Ministry of Communication and Aviation to draft national Data Protection and Privacy legislation under the Pacific E-commerce Initiative, in a project listed as active from July 2025 with no fixed end date. This builds on a national Data Protection and Privacy policy developed with UNCDF support and involves stakeholder consultations aimed at aligning with international standards while fitting local needs. Reported design features of the draft framework include an Office of the Privacy Commissioner and 72-hour breach notification, though no bill text has been published for verification.

In the meantime, protections are thin: there is no national framework for digital identity or data privacy, and the main adjacent instruments are the National Cybersecurity Policy launched in August 2024 and general confidentiality rules in sectoral legislation. There is no registration, breach notification or transfer regime, and no regulator to deal with.

For professionals, the practical takeaway is that the Solomon Islands is at drafting/consultation stage — earlier than a bill before Parliament — so any compliance obligations are at least one legislative cycle away. The 'consultation' label previously recorded remains accurate.

summary: Somalia enacted its first comprehensive privacy statute, the Data Protection Act (Law No. 005 of 2023), signed by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud on 21 March 2023 and effective from 23 March 2023. Modeled in significant part on modern African frameworks such as Nigeria's NDPA, it regulates collection, storage, processing and transfer of personal data across all sectors, and scales obligations by imposing the heaviest duties on 'controllers and processors of major importance'.

The Somali Data Protection Authority (DPA) was officially launched in February 2024 and is unusually active for a young regulator — publishing guidance, implementing regulations and e-services. Key obligations include 72-hour breach notification to the Authority, DPO appointment for government bodies and larger or sensitive-data processors, adequacy-or-safeguards rules for cross-border transfers, and parental consent for data of children under 18.

Penalties can reach a percentage (commentators cite 2–4%) of annual turnover, though enforcement is still building and implementing regulations continue to flesh out the regime. Somalia has no EU adequacy decision; the practical compliance picture depends heavily on DPA guidance.

summary: South Korea's Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), enacted in 2011 and heavily amended in 2020 and 2023, is one of Asia's strictest and most actively enforced privacy regimes. It applies to virtually all public and private data controllers, with extraterritorial reach over foreign companies serving Korean users. The independent Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) consolidates rulemaking, investigation and sanctioning powers, and has fined global tech companies tens of billions of won.

The 2023 amendment (effective from September 2023, with provisions phasing in through 2025) unified the previously separate online/offline rules, standardized breach notification at 72 hours, expanded cross-border transfer mechanisms beyond consent (adequacy designations, certifications, contractual disclosure), introduced rights around automated decision-making, and moved penalties to a turnover basis — up to 3% of total annual revenue, with the burden on the company to show revenue unrelated to the violation. In February 2026 the National Assembly went further, authorizing fines of up to 10% of total revenue for repeat, intentional, or mass-scale (10m+ subjects) breach cases, and tying accountability to senior management.

Distinctive features include mandatory designation of a privacy officer (CPO) for all controllers, guardian consent for children under 14, a domestic representative requirement for large foreign providers, and separate stringent rules for resident registration numbers and pseudonymized data. Korea has held an EU adequacy decision since December 2021, making it a reliable hub for EU data flows. Enforcement is real and frequent — this is a jurisdiction to treat with GDPR-level seriousness.
south-korea.xborder: Consent, contractual disclosure, PIPC adequacy designation, or approved certification

summary: South Sudan has no data protection law and no supervisory authority, but the picture is moving. The government announced that its first-ever Data Protection Bill would be introduced in 2026, to be drafted jointly by the ministries of information and justice as part of a push to have all cyberspace-governing laws in place — though as of August 2026 no tabled bill or published draft could be verified.

The country's flagship digital statute is instead the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act 2026, signed by President Salva Kiir on 18 February 2026 and now being enforced ahead of the December 2026 elections. It criminalises online fraud, harassment and harmful content, and includes some data-related offences, but it is a criminal statute — press-freedom groups including CPJ have warned it threatens journalists — not a data protection regime conferring rights on data subjects.

Beyond that, protections are limited to the constitutional right to privacy in the Transitional Constitution and scattered sectoral provisions. Organizations handling South Sudanese data face no domestic registration, DPO or breach duties today, but should watch for the promised Data Protection Bill later in 2026.

summary: Spain applies the GDPR directly, supplemented by Organic Law 3/2018 (LOPDGDD), which goes further than most member-state laws: beyond filling GDPR opening clauses it adds a catalogue of "digital rights" — digital disconnection at work, device privacy for employees, digital education, and rights concerning deceased persons' data. The digital consent age is set at 14, and Article 34 makes DPO appointment mandatory for 16 listed sectors (including banks, insurers, health centres, schools, telecoms and gambling operators) regardless of size, with appointments notified to the AEPD within 10 days.

The regulator is the AEPD, consistently among the most active supervisory authorities in Europe by volume of resolutions and fines, with major penalties against banks, telecoms and utilities. Spain also uses statutory presumptions (e.g. blocklist rules, video surveillance and workplace monitoring provisions in the LOPDGDD) that give enforcement a distinctly codified flavour compared with other member states.

Compliance is standard GDPR — lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, Chapter V transfers — plus the Spanish extras: check whether your sector triggers mandatory DPO designation, honour employees' digital rights, and apply the age-14 rule for minors' consent.
spain.xborder: Free flow within EU/EEA; GDPR Chapter V tools (adequacy, SCCs, BCRs) for third countries

summary: Sri Lanka's Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022 made it the first South Asian country to enact comprehensive, GDPR-style privacy legislation. It applies to controllers and processors in Sri Lanka and to those abroad offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Sri Lanka. The Act creates familiar duties — lawful bases for processing, data subject rights, DPO appointment for higher-risk processing, breach notification, and controlled cross-border transfers — overseen by a dedicated Data Protection Authority (DPA), established in 2023.

The critical caveat is timing: the Act is being commenced in phases. The institutional parts (establishing the DPA and its administration) are in force, but the substantive obligations in Parts I–III were postponed — the original 18 March 2025 commencement was repealed, and the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act No. 22 of 2025 pushed the timeline back while the DPA completes staffing, rules and guidance. As of mid-2026, no Gazette Order has yet brought the core obligations fully into operation, so day-to-day enforcement against controllers has not really begun.

For a meeting, the practical framing is: the law exists and the regulator is real and issuing circulars (e.g. on DPOs), but compliance deadlines are still crystallizing, with full effect expected during 2026. Penalties, once live, run to LKR 10 million per directive breach, doubling for repeat offences.
sri-lanka.xborder: Transfers permitted to adequacy-designated jurisdictions or with safeguards/consent; 2025 amendments relaxed data-location flexibility

summary: St. Kitts & Nevis occupies an unusual middle ground: the National Assembly passed the Data Protection Act, 2018 (Act No. 5 of 2018) on 4 May 2018 and it was gazetted in June 2018, but the Act only takes effect on a date fixed by the Minister for Justice by commencement order — and no such order has ever been published. As of the most recent authoritative reporting, the Act remains not in force, so there are no operative data protection obligations, no supervisory authority, and no enforcement.

The dormant Act follows the Caribbean/Commonwealth model (influenced by the OECS harmonization effort and similar to other regional Data Protection Acts), covering processing by public and private bodies, consent-based processing, security safeguards, and an Information Commissioner as regulator once commenced. Until then, privacy protection rests on the constitutional protection of privacy of home and property and on sectoral confidentiality rules (e.g., in financial services legislation).

For practical purposes the jurisdiction should be treated as having no enforceable general privacy law today, but with a ready-made statute that could be switched on quickly by ministerial order — worth monitoring for organizations in financial services and citizenship-by-investment sectors that handle large volumes of personal data.

summary: Saint Lucia enacted its Data Protection Act in 2011 (amended in 2015), but the law sat dormant for over a decade. In early 2023 the Government issued a proclamation order partially commencing the Act, bringing the core data protection principles — purpose limitation, accountability, adequacy of safeguards, fairness and transparency — into legal effect. So the recorded status of 'no law' is out of date: Saint Lucia now has an operative, if incomplete, data protection statute. It is a pre-GDPR-style framework covering controllers who process personal data in or from Saint Lucia, with a registration obligation and a Data Protection Commissioner as the oversight office.

Important gaps remain. Provisions granting individuals their operative rights — access, correction, and objection to processing — had not been proclaimed as of the last available reporting, and there is no public evidence of a fully staffed, operational Commissioner's office actively enforcing the law. Penalties are modest by modern standards (fines in the tens of thousands of EC dollars and short imprisonment terms, up to XCD 100,000 for companies), and there is no GDPR-style 72-hour breach notification or DPO mandate.

For practical purposes: businesses handling Saint Lucian personal data should comply with the in-force principles and prepare to register, but the enforcement risk is currently low and the regime should be monitored for the proclamation of the remaining provisions and the operationalisation of the Commissioner.
st-lucia.xborder: Transfers restricted unless adequate protection is ensured

summary: St. Vincent and the Grenadines has no comprehensive data protection law in force. The country enacted a Privacy Act in 2003, intended to regulate the collection, use, correction and disclosure of personal data held by public authorities, but the commencement order needed to bring it into operation has never been issued, so the Act remains unenforceable on paper more than two decades after passage. Even if commenced, its scope is largely limited to the public sector and it falls well short of a modern, GDPR-style framework.

There is no data protection authority, no registration regime, no breach notification duty and no administrative fining power. Practical privacy protection rests on general constitutional and common-law principles, and on sectoral confidentiality rules (for example in banking and the offshore financial services sector, which is significant to the local economy). Some organisations — notably financial institutions serving international clients — apply GDPR-derived policies voluntarily because of extraterritorial exposure.

For a meeting: treat SVG as a jurisdiction with a legal vacuum rather than a light-touch regime. Companies operating there are effectively governed by contractual commitments and any foreign laws (GDPR, etc.) that reach them, not by local statute. No active bill was identified as progressing through Parliament as of mid-2026.

sudan.notes: A 2018 draft bill exists on paper but has been dormant for years; the ongoing civil war makes any legislative progress unlikely.

summary: Sudan has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. A Draft Data Protection Bill was proposed in 2018 to set out rules for the collection, storage, processing and sharing of personal information, but it never advanced to enactment, and the legislative process has been effectively frozen — first by the 2021 coup and then by the civil war that broke out in April 2023 and was still ongoing as of 2026.

What exists instead is a patchwork of sectoral instruments: the Electronic Transactions Act 2007, the Cybercrime Act 2007 and the Cybercrime Prevention (Amendment) Act 2020, plus informational-crimes provisions. These laws criminalize certain misuse of computer systems and communications but do not create data-subject rights, controller obligations, or a supervisory regime. Constitutional privacy guarantees under the 2019 Constitutional Document are of limited practical effect given the collapse of transitional institutions.

For any organization handling Sudanese personal data, the practical position is that there are no registration, DPO, breach-notification or transfer rules to comply with domestically — but also no legal certainty. Expect no near-term movement on a data protection statute while the conflict continues.

suriname.notes: Information is sparse: the draft bill has been pending in the National Assembly since roughly 2020-2021 with no verified movement in 2025-2026, so 'draft in progress' may overstate current momentum.

summary: Suriname has no data protection law in force, but — unlike a pure 'nothing' jurisdiction — it has a draft bill formally before parliament, so its recorded status of 'none' undersells the position slightly. The Wet Bescherming Privacy en Persoonsgegevens (Privacy and Personal Data Protection Bill, circulated around 2020-2021) has been under consideration in De Nationale Assemblée, where it has been handled by the Commission of Rapporteurs, with stakeholder consultation rounds (including the ICT Association of Suriname) feeding written comments into the process. The bill would establish an independent data protection authority, data subject rights, and controller/processor obligations broadly in the modern mould.

Progress has been very slow: the bill has sat in the legislative process for years with no enacted outcome and no clear timeline as of 2025-2026. In the meantime, protection rests on general constitutional privacy principles and scattered sectoral confidentiality rules; there is no regulator, no registration, no breach duty and no fines regime. (Note that the Caribbean Netherlands 'BES' islands' privacy rules sometimes surfaced in searches are Dutch law and irrelevant to Suriname.)

For a meeting: treat Suriname as an unregulated jurisdiction with a long-stalled draft. Businesses handling Surinamese personal data are effectively bound only by contract and any extraterritorial foreign law, but should track the DNA's agenda since enactment would create a new authority and compliance regime from scratch.

summary: As an EU member state, Sweden is governed directly by the GDPR, supplemented by the Data Protection Act (2018:218) — 'the Act with supplementary provisions to the EU GDPR' (dataskyddslagen) — and the Data Protection Ordinance (2018:219), both in force since 25 May 2018. The national law exercises GDPR opening clauses, setting the digital age of consent at 13, regulating personal identity numbers, and preserving Sweden's strong constitutional protections for freedom of expression and press, which carve journalistic and constitutionally protected publishing out of much of the regime.

The supervisory authority is IMY (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten, the Swedish Authority for Privacy Protection), renamed from the Data Inspection Board (Datainspektionen) in January 2021. Sweden has one of the world's oldest data protection traditions — its first national data act dates to 1973 — and IMY actively audits, handles complaints and issues administrative fines, with a distinctive national cap of SEK 10 million for fines against public authorities.

Compliance for organisations operating in Sweden is essentially GDPR compliance: lawful basis, transparency, 72-hour breach notification, DPIAs, and Chapter V safeguards for transfers outside the EU/EEA.
