summary: Switzerland's fully revised Federal Act on Data Protection (revFADP), adopted in September 2020 and in force since 1 September 2023, modernised Swiss law to GDPR-comparable standards while keeping a distinctly Swiss design. It applies to private controllers and federal bodies, has extraterritorial effect on processing with effects in Switzerland, and requires foreign companies meeting thresholds to appoint a Swiss representative. The EU renewed Switzerland's adequacy status on 15 January 2024, so EU-Swiss data flows remain free.

The headline structural difference from the GDPR is sanctions: there are no corporate administrative fines. Instead, intentional violations of specific duties (information, disclosure, security, transfer rules) are criminal offences punishable by fines up to CHF 250,000 imposed on responsible individuals — managers, not companies — which changes personal risk calculations for executives. Breach notification runs to the FDPIC "as soon as possible" only where high risk is involved, and a DPO ("data protection advisor") is optional.

Compliance staples include records of processing (with an exemption for companies under 250 employees and low-risk processing), privacy by design and default, DPIAs for high-risk processing, and transfer checks against the Federal Council's country adequacy list. The FDPIC supervises and investigates but cannot itself levy fines; prosecution runs through cantonal criminal authorities.

summary: Syria has no comprehensive data protection or privacy law, and no bill for one is known to be in progress as of August 2026. Privacy protections are fragmentary: the Constitutional Declaration of 13 March 2025, issued by the transitional government after the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, contains general rights guarantees, and older sectoral rules (telecommunications regulation, banking secrecy, and general civil/criminal provisions on correspondence and defamation) provide narrow, uneven coverage.

The closest thing to data-related legislation is the Assad-era Cybercrime Law No. 20 of 2022, which criminalises certain misuse of information systems and online content but is primarily a speech-control instrument, with vague offences such as 'undermining the prestige of the state'. Human rights organisations — including Amnesty International and the Syrian Network for Human Rights — have documented its continued use by transitional authorities against journalists and activists through 2026. In June 2026 the Ministry of Justice announced a review of the law to harmonise it with the Constitutional Declaration and international standards, and introduced some limits on its use, but it remains in force.

For any organisation handling Syrian personal data, the practical position is that there is no supervisory authority, no registration, breach-notification or transfer regime, and no data-subject rights framework. Compliance decisions should be driven by the laws of the organisation's own jurisdiction (e.g. GDPR for EU entities), sanctions considerations, and heightened ethical duties of care given the acute risks that data exposure poses to individuals in Syria's transitional context.

summary: Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) is one of Asia's older comprehensive privacy laws — enacted in 1995 as the Computer-Processed Personal Data Protection Act, renamed and broadened in 2010, and in force since 2012. It applies to both government and non-government entities processing personal data of natural persons, covers all sectors, and grants data subjects rights of access, correction, deletion and objection. Historically its biggest weakness was fragmented enforcement: each sector ministry policed the Act within its own domain, with no central regulator.

That changed after a 2022 Constitutional Court ruling required an independent supervisory mechanism. A 2023 amendment raised fines (to NT$15 million for repeated security failures) and created a Preparatory Office of the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), which has operated since December 2023. Major amendments promulgated on 11 November 2025 formally establish the PDPC as an independent, centralized authority with interpretive, inspection and enforcement powers, mandate DPOs for government agencies, introduce breach reporting to the authority (a 72-hour regime), and move cross-border transfer restriction powers to the PDPC. The effective date of the 2025 amendments will be set by the Executive Yuan.

For businesses, Taiwan is a moderate-risk but tightening jurisdiction: fines were traditionally low, but the new PDPC, higher penalties, and mandatory breach reporting signal a shift toward GDPR-style centralized enforcement. Cross-border transfers remain generally free unless specifically restricted.

summary: Tajikistan enacted Law No. 1537 'On the Protection of Personal Data' on 3 August 2018, a CIS-model comprehensive statute governing collection, processing and protection of personal data by state bodies, legal entities and individuals. It follows the familiar regional template: consent as the default legal basis, purpose limitation, confidentiality duties on data holders/operators, and data subject rights to access and correct their data.

The law provides for an 'authorized state body' on personal data protection, determined by the President, which is meant to implement state policy, issue implementing acts, and handle complaints — including imposing administrative penalties. However, no independent, operational data protection authority with a public enforcement record has emerged, and practical guidance on procedures such as database registration is scarce.

For businesses, the compliance reality is consent-driven paperwork rather than active regulatory scrutiny. There is no DPO requirement and no breach notification regime. Cross-border transfers follow the CIS pattern of permitting transfers to jurisdictions ensuring adequate protection, with consent as the practical fallback.

summary: Tanzania's Personal Data Protection Act, 2022 (Act No. 11 of 2022, passed 27 November 2022, in force 1 May 2023) established the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) and, together with the May 2023 Regulations on collection/processing and complaints handling, created a complete operative regime. The framework's defining feature is gatekeeping: controllers and processors must register with the PDPC before processing any personal data, and cross-border transfers require a prior PDPC permit backed by adequacy findings, international or bilateral agreements, or contractual safeguards.

Obligations include appointing a data protection officer, notifying the Commission of security breaches without undue delay, and observing GDPR-style processing principles and data subject rights. Sanctions are layered: administrative enforcement and penalty notices up to TZS 100 million plus uncapped compensation orders, and criminal offences (such as unlawful disclosure) carrying fines up to TZS 5 billion for corporates and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals.

Enforcement has moved from theory to practice quickly. Registration deadlines were extended through 2025, with the PDPC signaling full enforcement against unregistered processors from April 2026; the Commission has also begun issuing substantive decisions — notably a 2025 ruling that children's images are sensitive personal data whose commercial use without parental consent is unlawful. Any business touching Tanzanian personal data in 2026 should treat registration, DPO appointment and transfer permits as immediate, actively-policed requirements.

summary: Thailand's Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019), fully effective since 1 June 2022, is a GDPR-inspired law covering private and most public-sector processing, with extraterritorial reach over foreign businesses offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Thailand. It requires a lawful basis for processing, with a strong emphasis on explicit, unbundled consent, and grants data subjects rights to access, correction, erasure, portability and objection.

The Office of the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) has built out the regime through sub-regulations and guidelines on consent, notification, breach reporting, DPOs and cross-border transfers. Distinctive features include a detailed minor-consent framework tied to the Civil and Commercial Code (guardian consent below age 10, dual consent for minors 10–20) and a 72-hour breach notification rule with a formal exemption-request process for late filings.

Enforcement moved from a soft-touch phase into real sanctions: the PDPC issued its first administrative fines and in August 2025 imposed penalties totalling over THB 21.5 million, signalling the end of the grace-period approach. Administrative fines run to THB 5 million per violation, alongside criminal liability and statutory/punitive damages in civil claims.

summary: Timor-Leste has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. The main protections are constitutional: Article 38 of the Constitution gives citizens the right to access their personal data held in manual or electronic records, to demand rectification, and to know the purpose of collection, while related articles protect privacy of the home and correspondence. There is no statute operationalizing these rights against private-sector processing.

Movement is finally visible, but through a cybersecurity route rather than a standalone privacy bill. In July 2026 the Government submitted to the National Parliament a request for legislative authorisation to approve a cybersecurity legislative package — covering cybercrime, digital evidence, a national cybersecurity authority, and rules on the protection of personal data and privacy. Civil society has criticized earlier drafts of the cyber law over online-freedom and data protection concerns, and the package had not been enacted as of August 2026.

Practically, organizations operating in Timor-Leste face no registration, breach notification, or transfer restrictions today, but should track the cybersecurity package, since its personal data provisions would create the country's first enforceable data rules.

summary: Togo's Law No. 2019-014 of 29 October 2019 is a GDPR-inspired framework governing the collection, processing, transmission, storage and use of personal data. It rests on principles of consent and legitimacy, lawfulness, accuracy, transparency, confidentiality and security, and applies broadly to public and private controllers processing data in Togo. Outside limited exemptions, processing must be declared in advance to the supervisory authority, which issues a receipt; transfers of data abroad require the authority's authorization.

The supervisory authority, the Instance de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (IPDCP), took years to materialise: its president, Lt-Col Bédiani Béléi, was appointed by presidential decree in September 2024 and the authority was officially launched on 28 March 2025. It is now standing up its operational committees, running awareness campaigns and beginning to accompany businesses and administrations toward compliance — so active enforcement is only just starting.

Violations can attract fines up to XOF 10 million and/or prison terms of up to five years. Togo has no EU adequacy decision; practitioners should watch for IPDCP implementing decisions and compliance formalities now that the regulator is live.

summary: Tonga moved from having no data protection law at all to a comprehensive, GDPR-style regime with the Privacy Act 2025 (Act 34 of 2025), which received Royal Assent from King Tupou VI on 16 December 2025 and was published in the Government Gazette in early January 2026 alongside a companion Personal Health Information Protection Act 2025. The Act protects 'personal information' with definitions closely modelled on the GDPR (including sensitive categories such as biometric and genetic data), applies to data controllers and processors established in Tonga or processing within the Kingdom, and reaches offshore entities that target goods or services at, or monitor, people in Tonga. It binds the State, though public authorities enjoy broad carve-outs for national security, law enforcement and public-safety research, and there are exemptions for personal/household use and journalism.

The Act creates an independent Privacy Commission — a body corporate run by a single Privacy Commissioner chosen through an open, merit-based Appointments Committee process — with powers to investigate complaints, issue enforcement notices and information notices, accept enforceable undertakings, designate countries or contractual clauses as adequate for cross-border transfers, and enter and search premises. Controllers must have a lawful basis for processing (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task or legitimate interests), give detailed collection notices, minimise and secure data, limit retention, and put written agreements in place with processors. Data subjects get rights of access, correction, deletion, direct-marketing opt-out, objection, consent withdrawal and protection against solely automated decisions; portability can be added by regulation. Enforcement is civil-court based rather than administrative: the Commission or Attorney-General sues for pecuniary penalties capped at TOP 100,000 for repeat corporate contraventions.

Enforcement reality is the key caveat for any meeting: the Act commences 'on a date proclaimed by Cabinet' (s.1(2)), and while local reporting treats the gazetted 2025 Acts as now law, no Cabinet commencement proclamation, Commissioner appointment or functioning Commission could be independently verified as of August 2026. The 72-hour breach-notification duty is expressly deferred until two years after commencement, and registration, impact assessments and portability all await ministerial regulations. Practically, organisations handling Tongan personal data should treat the Act as the operative standard and prepare now, but should not expect active supervision in the immediate term. Tonga holds no EU adequacy decision.

summary: Trinidad and Tobago's Data Protection Act, 2011 (Chap. 22:04) is on the books but only fragmentarily in force — a critical caveat behind its 'has a law' label. Part I and sections 7-18, 22, 23, 25(1), 26 and 28 were proclaimed on 6 January 2012, essentially the definitional and administrative machinery including the Office of the Information Commissioner; sections 42(a) and (b) followed on 20 August 2021. The operative parts — the rules actually governing collection, protection and disclosure of personal information, and the penalties for breaking them — have never been proclaimed. In practice, there is no enforceable general obligation on private-sector controllers, no registration, no breach notification duty, and no functioning enforcement regime.

When (if) fully proclaimed, the Act would impose General Privacy Principles on public and private bodies, overseen by the Information Commissioner, with penalties of up to TTD 100,000 or five years' imprisonment for individuals and up to 10% of annual returns for companies. A 2018 government review found the Act out of step with the GDPR (weak on e-marketing, online privacy and breach notification), and stakeholder consultations in 2019 discussed amendments; parliamentary motions have since urged proclamation of the remaining sections, but as of 2025-2026 the position was unchanged.

For a meeting: treat T&T as 'law enacted, obligations mostly dormant'. Compliance exposure today comes mainly from sectoral confidentiality rules, contract, and foreign laws with extraterritorial reach — but reform or proclamation could change the picture, so the Act's GDPR-divergent text is still worth knowing.

summary: Tunisia was the first Arab country to adopt comprehensive data protection legislation: Organic Act No. 2004-63 of 27 July 2004, which establishes general principles of lawful processing, data subject rights, and the independent supervisory authority, the INPDP. The regime rests on prior formalities — declarations to the INPDP before processing, with authorizations needed for certain categories — and treats children's data with unusual care, involving guardian consent and judicial oversight.

The 2004 Act is now widely regarded as outdated, and a full replacement is in progress. A GDPR-inspired organic bill of 123 articles — covering processing principles, data subject rights (including portability and erasure), a strengthened supervisory authority, high-risk processing rules relevant to AI, and deterrent sanctions — was under examination by the Rights and Freedoms Committee of the Assembly of People's Representatives as of early 2026, but had not been reported as finally adopted.

In practice, enforcement under the 2004 Act relies on criminal-style penalties rather than large administrative fines, and the INPDP has historically been more visible in advocacy and opinions than in heavy sanctions. Businesses meeting professionals should assume the 2004 declaration regime applies today while planning for a significantly stricter GDPR-style law once the pending bill passes.

summary: Turkey's Law No. 6698 on the Protection of Personal Data (KVKK), in force since 2016, was modelled on the pre-GDPR EU Directive but was substantially modernised by the March 2024 amendments (Law 7499, the '8th Judicial Reform Package'), effective June 2024. The law applies to anyone processing personal data of individuals in Turkey and is enforced by the Personal Data Protection Authority and its decision-making Board in Ankara.

Turkey's most distinctive feature is VERBIS, the mandatory public registry of data controllers: Turkish controllers above employee/turnover thresholds and all foreign controllers processing Turkish personal data must register and appoint a contact person (Turkey does not mandate a GDPR-style DPO). The 2024 reform overhauled the previously restrictive cross-border transfer regime — which had effectively required explicit consent or Board permission — replacing it with a GDPR-like structure of adequacy decisions, Turkish Standard Contractual Clauses (which must be filed with the Authority within five business days of signing), and Binding Corporate Rules. It also expanded the legal bases for processing sensitive data, notably for employment purposes.

Enforcement is vigorous and fines are indexed annually for inflation: 2026 amounts reach TRY 17,092,242 per violation, with VERBIS failures alone drawing fines from TRY 341,809 upward. Breach notification to the Board is due within 72 hours under Board decision 2019/10, plus notification to affected individuals. Multinationals should treat Turkey as a distinct compliance regime — GDPR compliance helps but does not cover VERBIS registration, Turkish-language SCC filing, or local sensitive-data rules.

summary: Turkmenistan's data protection framework rests on Law No. 519-V 'On Information about Private Life and its Protection', adopted on 20 March 2017 and in force since 1 July 2017. It is the country's only law dedicated to the collection and processing of personal data, and it partially mirrors principles familiar from the GDPR — lawfulness, purpose limitation, consent as the main processing basis, and confidentiality/security duties on operators of personal data databases.

The most distinctive feature is what is missing: there is no dedicated supervisory authority. Oversight sits generally with the Cabinet of Ministers, with the Prosecutor General's Office responsible for supervision of legality. There is no database registration requirement, no data protection officer requirement, and no breach notification regime. Cross-border transfers are contemplated where the receiving state ensures protection of the data.

In practice, enforcement is essentially invisible: no public enforcement actions, guidance, or case law are available, and the state itself operates pervasive surveillance with tight information controls. Companies dealing with Turkmenistan should treat the law as a formal baseline with little practical regulatory activity, and rely on consent and contractual protections.

summary: Tuvalu has no data protection or privacy legislation. UNCTAD's assessments state plainly that no legal framework exists for electronic transactions, data protection or online consumer protection in Tuvalu; a cybercrime law is the main piece of digital-era legislation. No supervisory authority exists and no bill could be verified as under parliamentary consideration as of August 2026.

The direction of travel is set by UNCTAD's eTrade readiness assessment (launched December 2019), which proposed a roadmap for a digital economy development agenda including foundational e-commerce laws — of which data protection would be one pillar. Tuvalu participates in regional Pacific digital-policy and cybersecurity discussions, but with a population of around 11,000 and severe capacity constraints, legislative progress has been slow.

Note that some low-quality secondary websites claim Tuvalu has a 'Data Protection and Privacy Act 2020' and a 'Tuvalu Data Protection Authority'; no official or authoritative source corroborates this, and UNCTAD's own reporting contradicts it. Treat such claims as erroneous.

summary: Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 (now Cap. 97) is one of East Africa's established regimes, fleshed out by the Data Protection and Privacy Regulations, 2021. It applies to anyone collecting or processing personal data of Ugandan residents — including offshore entities, as the regulator clarified in 2025 guidance — and is supervised by the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO), an office established under NITA-U that has grown into an active regulator.

The regime is registration-heavy: every data collector, processor and controller must register with the PDPO through its online portal, and registration must be renewed annually — failure to register is itself an offence. Cross-border transfers are permitted only with the data subject's consent or where the receiving jurisdiction provides protection at least equivalent to the Act, and controllers must keep records justifying each transfer for inspection.

Enforcement has moved from theory to practice, with the PDPO issuing registration decisions, its first fines, and Uganda recording criminal data protection convictions in 2025. Corporate offenders face fines up to 2% of annual gross turnover on conviction, alongside individual fines and potential imprisonment. Uganda holds no EU adequacy decision.
uganda.xborder: Allowed with data subject consent or where the destination offers protection at least equivalent to the Act

summary: Ukraine's framework is still the Law on Personal Data Protection No. 2297-VI, adopted on 1 June 2010 and in force since 1 January 2011. It is a pre-GDPR, Convention 108-style law applying to controllers and processors handling personal data of individuals in Ukraine. Since 2014 supervision has sat with the Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman) rather than a dedicated data protection authority — an unusual arrangement the pending reform would end.

The law requires a legal basis for processing, notification of high-risk processing to the Ombudsman, designation of a responsible person for such processing, and observance of data subject rights. Enforcement is real but light: the Ombudsman investigates complaints and conducts inspections, but fines under the Code of Administrative Offences top out around UAH 34,000 (under EUR 1,000), so reputational and criminal exposure matter more than administrative penalties.

The big story is reform: Draft Law No. 8153 passed its first reading on 20 November 2024 and, as of mid-2026, remains in preparation for a second reading. It would align Ukraine with the GDPR and Convention 108+, create an independent supervisory authority, add 72-hour breach notification and DPO duties, and introduce fines up to UAH 150 million or 8% of annual turnover. EU accession pressure makes eventual adoption likely, so anyone building compliance in Ukraine should plan against GDPR-grade requirements.
ukraine.xborder: Free to EEA and Convention 108 states; others need adequate protection, consent or listed grounds

summary: The UAE's first federal data protection law, Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 (PDPL), has been in force since 2 January 2022. It applies to controllers and processors in the UAE (outside the financial free zones) and to those abroad processing data of UAE residents, and it follows a broadly GDPR-like architecture: lawful bases centered on consent with exceptions, data subject rights, DPO requirements for high-risk processing, breach notification to a federal Data Office, and adequacy-or-safeguards rules for international transfers. The DIFC, ADGM and Dubai Healthcare City free zones each retain their own separate data protection laws and regulators.

The regime's defining feature is its unfinished state. The Executive Regulations that must operationalize the PDPL — and the Cabinet decision fixing administrative penalties — had still not been issued as of the Chambers Data Protection & Privacy 2026 guide, which describes them as 'a work in progress,' and the UAE Data Office (created by Federal Decree-Law No. 44 of 2021) is not yet fully operational, with the TDRA and Digital Government providing transitional support. Organizations will get six months from publication of the regulations to come into compliance.

Enforcement reality is therefore limited: compliance is driven by internal risk management, sector regulators (Central Bank, health authorities, TDRA) and the active free-zone regimes rather than federal PDPL enforcement. Note that a number of 2026 marketing-oriented sources claim the Executive Regulations have now been issued and enforcement activated; this could not be verified against authoritative legal sources and should be independently confirmed.

summary: Post-Brexit, the UK runs a retained-EU-law regime: the UK GDPR (the EU GDPR as domesticated) together with the Data Protection Act 2018 and PECR. This framework is now being amended — not replaced — by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA), which received Royal Assent on 19 June 2025 and is being commenced in phases through June 2026, with a major tranche of data protection provisions in force from 5 February 2026. DUAA introduces 'recognised legitimate interests', relaxed rules on some cookies and on automated decision-making, a new statutory complaints-handling duty on controllers (from June 2026), and restructures the ICO into an 'Information Commission'.

The regime applies to any organisation established in the UK or targeting people there. The ICO is a globally prominent regulator that supervises via audits, enforcement notices and fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of worldwide turnover; most controllers must pay an annual data protection fee, which funds the office. The digital age of consent is 13, reinforced by the ICO's influential Age Appropriate Design (Children's) Code.

Crucially for international business, the European Commission renewed the UK's two adequacy decisions on 19 December 2025 — after concluding the DUAA keeps UK protection 'essentially equivalent' to EU standards — so personal data continues to flow freely between the EU/EEA and the UK until 27 December 2031.
united-kingdom.xborder: UK adequacy regulations for approved countries; otherwise IDTA or UK Addendum to EU SCCs

summary: The United States still has no comprehensive federal privacy law. Protection comes from a patchwork: sectoral federal statutes (HIPAA, GLBA, COPPA, FCRA), FTC enforcement of unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act, and a fast-growing layer of state comprehensive privacy laws. As of mid-2026, 25 states have enacted comprehensive consumer privacy laws — about 20 in effect and five more (Oklahoma, Alabama, Louisiana, Georgia, Vermont) taking effect in 2027–2028 — most following the Virginia model of notice, consumer rights, opt-outs for sale/targeted advertising, and consent for sensitive data. California remains the outlier with its own dedicated regulator (CPPA) and rulemaking.

Federal legislation remains at the bill stage: the American Privacy Rights Act expired with the 118th Congress in January 2025, and new comprehensive proposals — the SECURE Data Act and GUARD Financial Data Act, introduced in April 2026 — are pending with uncertain prospects. Separately, the DOJ's bulk sensitive data rule (under Executive Order 14117) now restricts transfers of Americans' sensitive data to countries of concern, a national-security-driven form of export control rather than privacy law.

For EU transfers, the EU–US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision (July 2023) remains in force: the EU General Court upheld it in Latombe v Commission in September 2025, though an appeal to the CJEU is pending. Enforcement reality is active but fragmented — FTC consent decrees, state AG actions, and California CPPA orders — so multistate businesses typically build to the strictest applicable state standard.
united-states.xborder: No general restriction; DOJ bulk sensitive data rule (2025) restricts transfers to countries of concern

summary: Uruguay's Law 18.331 of 2008 is one of Latin America's most European-style data protection laws, and it earned Uruguay an EU adequacy decision in August 2012 (Decision 2012/484/EU) — reaffirmed by the European Commission on 15 January 2024. The law covers public and private processing, treats data protection as an inherent human right, and provides the habeas data action alongside administrative enforcement.

The regime has been actively modernized without a wholesale rewrite: Law 19.670 (2018) and its implementing Decree 64/020 (2020) grafted GDPR-style accountability onto the 2008 statute — mandatory data protection officers for public bodies and for private entities that process sensitive data as their core business or handle large volumes, 72-hour breach notification to the URCDP, proactive responsibility (privacy by design, impact assessments), and extended territorial scope.

The URCDP, a technically autonomous unit operating within the e-government agency AGESIC, is a credible and consultative regulator: it maintains database, DPO and breach registers, issues opinions and rulings, and sanctions range from warnings to fines of up to 500,000 indexed units plus database closure. For a small market, Uruguay punches above its weight as a compliant hub for regional data operations.
uruguay.xborder: Transfers only to countries with adequate protection or with safeguards (contract clauses) or consent (Art. 23)

summary: Uzbekistan's Law No. ZRU-547 'On Personal Data', adopted 2 July 2019 and in force since 1 October 2019, is the country's first comprehensive data protection statute. It applies to state bodies and private operators alike, requires consent or another legal basis for processing, and obliges most operators to register their personal data databases with the Personalization Agency under the Ministry of Justice — a notification-style filing decided within 15 days, with exemptions for employment data, publicly available data and several other categories. Operators must also designate a responsible person or unit for data protection.

The law became internationally notorious for its 2021 data localization amendment, which required personal data of Uzbek citizens processed via information technologies to be stored on servers physically located in Uzbekistan, enforced through a special register and website blocking (applied at times to major foreign platforms). That regime was substantially dismantled by amendments in force from 27 March 2026: storage and processing abroad is now permitted provided information security requirements and international data protection standards are met, clearing the path for cross-border digital services.

Enforcement is administered by the Personalization Agency alongside telecom inspection bodies, with penalties that are modest in monetary terms (base-calculation-value fines and possible criminal liability) but operationally significant through blocking powers. For foreign businesses the practical agenda is database registration, appointing a responsible person, and tracking the new 2026 cross-border conditions.

summary: Vanuatu now has a comprehensive data protection law in force — a status change from 'bill in progress'. The Data Protection and Privacy Act No. 13 of 2024 received assent on 5 December 2024 and commenced on 2 January 2025. It applies to public and private sectors, to processing within Vanuatu or of data generated/collected in Vanuatu wherever processed, and extraterritorially to foreign controllers offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Vanuatu. It follows GDPR architecture: processing principles (fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security), lawful bases including consent and legitimate interests, prohibitions on special-category and children's data with narrow exceptions, and data subject rights to access (free, within one month), restriction, rectification/erasure, objection, and freedom from solely automated decisions.

Two features stand out. First, the cross-border regime is unusually strict on paper: personal data generated or collected in Vanuatu must not be used elsewhere without prior authorisation from the Minister on the recommendation of the Deputy Commissioner of Data Protection and Privacy, unless the destination is on a Ministerial whitelist of adequate countries — a government-permission model rather than the GDPR's self-assessed safeguards. Second, enforcement is criminal rather than administrative: non-compliance with any provision is an offence punishable by fines up to VT 10 million (~USD 80,000), with no GDPR-style turnover-based administrative penalties.

Enforcement reality lags the text: the Deputy Commissioner sits within the Digital Safety Authority created by a companion Act, and that authority was not yet operational as of the latest available reporting; key operational details — breach notification duties and deadlines, processor obligations, records of processing — are delegated to Regulations that had not been issued. Businesses touching Vanuatu data should implement the principles and transfer controls now, and watch for the Regulations and the authority standing up.
vanuatu.xborder: Data generated or collected in Vanuatu cannot be used elsewhere without prior Ministerial authorisation on the Deputy Commissioner's recommendation, unless the destination country/organisation is on a prescribed whitelist (ss 15–17)

summary: Venezuela has no comprehensive data protection law and no data protection authority. Privacy protection rests on scattered instruments: Article 28 of the 1999 Constitution guarantees habeas data — the right to access one's personal data held in public or private registries and to seek correction or destruction — alongside Article 60's general privacy right and the secrecy of communications. A 2011 Constitutional Chamber (Supreme Tribunal) decision articulated data-processing principles drawn from these provisions, but they have never been implemented in a general statute.

What exists is sectoral: the Law on Data Messages and Electronic Signatures (2001), banking-sector confidentiality rules under the Law on Banking Sector Institutions (2014), the Infogobierno framework for state IT, and criminal provisions in the Special Law Against Computer Crimes. There is no DPO requirement, no registration, no breach notification duty, no administrative fines regime and no regulator to complain to. Major incidents — including the Movistar Venezuela breach in 2025 and the Cashea app breach in 2026 — have highlighted how little recourse affected individuals have beyond constitutional actions before courts of uneven independence.

For a meeting: assume no local compliance framework, but also high country risk around data handling — state surveillance concerns, weak rule of law, and the possibility that foreign regimes (GDPR, etc.) supply the applicable rules for any Venezuela-related processing. No serious draft data protection bill was identified as advancing in the National Assembly.

summary: Vietnam replaced its decree-level regime (Decree 13/2023, the 'PDPD') with a full statute: the Law on Personal Data Protection, No. 91/2025/QH15 (PDPL), passed on 26 June 2025 and effective 1 January 2026, together with guiding Decree 356/2025/ND-CP issued 31 December 2025. The PDPL applies to domestic and foreign organizations processing personal data of individuals in Vietnam, regardless of nationality, and establishes core rights to be informed, consent, access, and rectification.

Enforcement sits with the Ministry of Public Security through its cybersecurity department A05 rather than an independent DPA — a distinctive feature that colors the whole regime. The law keeps Vietnam's hallmark dossier system: organizations must prepare processing impact assessments and cross-border transfer impact assessments and lodge them with the MPS within 60 days, and notify breaches within 72 hours. Children's data requires guardian consent plus the child's own consent from age seven.

Sanctions were significantly hardened: statutory administrative fines up to VND 3 billion (about USD 115,000) for most violations, and for cross-border transfer breaches up to 5% of the prior year's revenue — among the toughest revenue-linked penalties in ASEAN. Businesses tracking Vietnam should update anything still referencing Decree 13/PDPD 2023.
vietnam.xborder: Permitted, but a transfer impact assessment dossier must be prepared and submitted to the MPS within 60 days of the first transfer

summary: Yemen has no data protection law, no draft bill in meaningful progress, and no supervisory authority. Privacy is addressed only in fragments: Article 52 of the Constitution guarantees the sanctity of private correspondence and postal, telephonic and electronic communications, which may be monitored or intercepted only under a legal warrant; the Penal Code and criminal procedure rules touch on privacy of the home and correspondence; and telecommunications regulation obliges licensed operators to keep customer communications confidential.

The most relevant modern statute is Law No. 13 of 2012 on the Right of Access to Information, which is a freedom-of-information law rather than a data protection law, though it contains some limits on disclosure of personal information held by public bodies. Civil society assessments (e.g., SAM for Rights and Liberties) consistently conclude that Yemen lacks any dedicated legislation protecting or organizing users' data against misuse by public or private actors.

The ongoing armed conflict and the split between rival authorities in Sana'a and Aden make new national legislation and any enforcement infrastructure unrealistic in the near term. Organizations handling data of Yemeni individuals should apply their own group-level standards, as there is no local compliance framework, regulator or breach-notification duty to satisfy.

summary: Zambia's Data Protection Act, 2021 (Act No. 3 of 2021) is a GDPR-influenced statute with a distinctly strict local flavor: it imposes mandatory registration of controllers and processors, mandatory DPO appointment, a 24-hour breach-notification window (among the world's tightest), and hard data-localization rules — sensitive personal data must be stored and processed inside Zambia, and even non-sensitive data can leave only with data-subject consent plus Commissioner-approved contracts, intragroup schemes, ministerial prescription or specific authorization. It applies extraterritorially to anyone processing the personal data of people in Zambia.

For several years the law outpaced its institutions — a Commissioner was appointed in 2023 but the office wasn't functional. That changed decisively: the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) is now fully operational, launched an online registration portal at dataprotection.gov.zm, and set a registration deadline of 30 April 2025, with non-registration punishable by a ZMW 200,000 fine and/or up to five years' imprisonment. General penalties scale to 2% of annual turnover for bodies corporate.

Practically, 2025–2026 marks Zambia's shift from legislative intent to regulatory action. Businesses — including foreign SaaS, fintech and telecom providers serving Zambian users — should confirm ODPC registration, appoint a DPO, map where sensitive data is hosted (localization is the most commercially disruptive requirement), and build 24-hour breach response into incident plans.
zambia.xborder: Sensitive personal data must be stored and processed in Zambia; other data transferable only with consent plus Commissioner-approved contracts, adequacy or authorization

summary: Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07], enacted in December 2021 and effective from 11 March 2022, is a hybrid statute combining cybercrime offences with a data protection regime. The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ) doubles as the Data Protection Authority. The Act covers lawful processing, data security, sensitive data, breach notification and cross-border transfers, though its data-subject rights are narrower than the GDPR's.

The regime hardened considerably with Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024 (Cyber and Data Protection — Licensing of Data Controllers and Appointment of Data Protection Officers — Regulations), promulgated 13 September 2024. Every data controller must obtain a data protection licence from POTRAZ (applications were due within six months, by 12 March 2025) and appoint a POTRAZ-certified DPO. Breach notification is unusually tight: 24 hours to POTRAZ, with high-risk breaches communicated to affected individuals within 72 hours.

Enforcement reality: POTRAZ has been actively driving licensing and DPO certification since 2024–25, making Zimbabwe one of the more operationally demanding regimes in the region. Penalties are criminal (fines up to level 11 on the standard scale and/or up to seven years' imprisonment for serious offences). Civil-society observers have raised concerns that the Act's cybercrime provisions can be used against journalists and critics, so the law cuts both ways politically.
zimbabwe.xborder: Notify POTRAZ before transfers; adequacy required, else explicit consent or contractual necessity
